metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer (TaT1 and CIS)
metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the clinical management of non-muscle-invasive bladder urothelial carcinoma, including Ta and T1 tumours and carcinoma in situ. It covers diagnosis, pathological classification, prediction of recurrence and progression, risk-adapted treatment, management after intravesical therapy failure, and follow-up. It also discusses treatment-related adverse effects, quality indicators and options for reducing interventions in selected patients.

conditions_covered: CIS in the upper urinary tract
target_population: patients suspected of having bladder cancer
patients with TaT1 tumours or carcinoma in situ
patients with primary or recurrent NMIBC
patients with recurrence during or after intravesical therapy

toxicities.event: Serious adverse effects of intravesical BCG
recognition: Symptoms may arise from BCG treatment or from bladder disease itself.
Delayed hypersensitivity can rarely appear years after treatment has ended.
prevention: Observe the contraindications to intravesical BCG because systemic absorption can cause major complications.
toxicities.dose_modifications: A maintenance schedule was not associated with more adverse effects than induction alone. In the EORTC study, one-third dose did not reduce toxicity relative to full-dose BCG and was associated with more recurrences, particularly when administered for only one year. A reduction to one-sixth dose lowered efficacy without lowering toxicity. A meta-analysis of nine RCTs found fewer adverse events, but more recurrences, with less than half of the standard dose.

recognition: Cystitis symptoms can persist or worsen after an instillation.

management.actions: Use Phenazopyridine, propantheline bromide or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Continue instillations if symptoms improve within a few days.
Defer the instillation, obtain a urine culture and begin empirical antibiotic treatment.

If the culture is positive, adjust antibiotics to susceptibility results. If it is negative, use quinolones* and consider daily analgesic anti-inflammatory instillations for five days; repeat the cycle if needed.

management.severity: No response to treatment and/or contracted bladder

toxicities.dose_modifications: Postpone BCG instillation when symptoms persist or worsen.

recognition: Haematuria; accompanying symptoms may raise concern for haemorrhagic cystitis.

management.actions: Obtain a urine culture to exclude haemorrhagic cystitis.
Perform cystoscopy to assess for a bladder tumour.

prevention: Do not administer intravesical BCG to patients with visible haematuria.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Visible haematuria is an absolute contraindication to a BCG instillation; nonvisible haematuria is not.

management.actions: Obtain a urine culture and give quinolones.
Give isoniazid (300 mg/day) and rifampicin (600 mg/day) for three months.
Obtain a urine culture and administer quinolones.

management.severity: Abscess or failure to respond to treatment

recognition: General malaise or fever after an instillation.

management.actions: These manifestations generally resolve within 48 hours, with or without antipyretics.

toxicities.incidence: Described as a rare complication; no percentage is given.
recognition: Arthralgia or reactive arthritis; the guideline regards this complication as an autoimmune reaction.

management.actions: Proceed to corticosteroids, high-dose quinolones or anti-tuberculosis drugs.
Immediately obtain a urine culture, blood tests and chest X-ray. Promptly start more than two antimicrobial agents while investigating the cause, and consult an infectious diseases specialist.

Give high-dose quinolones or isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol 1.2 g daily for six months. Start high-dose corticosteroids early and continue while symptoms persist. Consider an empirical non-specific antibiotic covering Gram-negative bacteria and/or Enterococcus.

prevention: Start BCG at least two weeks after transurethral resection of the bladder, provided haematuria has no signs or symptoms.
Respect the absolute contraindications to BCG instillation.

management.actions: Consider high-dose quinolones or isoniazid and rifampicin.

toxicities.dose_modifications: Delay therapy until the reaction resolves.

toxicities.incidence: BCG infections occurred in 1% after BCG instillations in a registry-based cohort. In a Swedish nationwide database of 5,033 patients exposed to BCG, the cumulative incidence of a reported tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis was 1.1 % at five years; incidence was highest in the first two years.
recognition: In the Swedish database, women had a lower incidence of reported tuberculosis than men.
prevention: Do not administer BCG during the first two weeks after TURB, in the presence of visible haematuria or symptomatic urinary tract infection, or after traumatic catheterisation.

recognition: The guideline reports severe complications following drug extravasation without specifying their clinical manifestations.
prevention: Omit the immediate single chemotherapy instillation when bladder perforation is evident or suspected, or when bleeding requires bladder irrigation.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Do not give the immediate single instillation under those conditions.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not needed solely because a patient receiving BCG has leukocyturia, nonvisible haematuria or asymptomatic bacteriuria; these findings do not contraindicate BCG.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients receiving intravesical BCG who have leukocyturia, nonvisible haematuria or asymptomatic bacteriuria

prophylaxis.recommendation: Begin intravesical BCG at least two weeks after transurethral resection of the bladder, if haematuria has no signs or symptoms. BCG instillation is absolutely contraindicated during the first two weeks after TURB, with visible haematuria, after traumatic catheterisation or with symptomatic urinary tract infection.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients being considered for intravesical BCG
prophylaxis.duration: At least two weeks after transurethral resection of the bladder before starting BCG

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not give an immediate single intravesical chemotherapy instillation if bladder perforation is overt or suspected, or if bleeding necessitates bladder irrigation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients being considered for an immediate chemotherapy instillation after TURB

infection_management.prevention: Start BCG at least two weeks after transurethral resection of the bladder if haematuria has no signs or symptoms, and observe the contraindications to instillation.
infection_management.management: Stop BCG. For severe infection, give high-dose quinolones or isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol 1.2 g daily for six months; start high-dose corticosteroids early for as long as symptoms persist. Consider an empirical non-specific antibiotic covering Gram-negative bacteria and/or Enterococcus.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Persistent severe cystitis symptoms associated with BCG and possible complicated UTI
infection_management.management: If symptoms persist or worsen, delay BCG, obtain a urine culture and start empirical antibiotics. Adjust treatment to susceptibility results when the culture is positive. If symptoms continue despite antibiotics and the culture is negative, use quinolones* and consider daily analgesic anti-inflammatory instillations for five days, repeating the cycle if necessary. The guideline notes a high risk of underlying complicated UTI even with a negative culture and states that the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee of the EMA restriction does not apply to empirical quinolones in this situation.

infection_management.prevention: Do not administer intravesical BCG while a symptomatic urinary tract infection is present.

infection_management.management: If haematuria after BCG accompanies other symptoms, obtain a urine culture to exclude haemorrhagic cystitis.

infection_management.prevention: The role of prophylactic anti-tuberculosis medication in immunocompromised patients remains unclear.

therapies_index.name: TURB
approved_indications: Diagnostic assessment and initial treatment when bladder cancer is suspected.
Removal of visible TaT1 bladder tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Resect all visible lesions and submit the specimens for pathological assessment.
monitoring: Document whether resection is complete, whether detrusor muscle is present, and any complications.
Perform the first follow-up cystoscopy three months after TURB in patients with TaT1 tumours or CIS.

therapies_index.name: en-bloc resection
approved_indications: Resection of selected exophytic bladder tumours.
therapies_index.administration: May use monopolar or bipolar current, Thulium-YAG, Holmium-YAG or KTP-Green Light lasers; feasibility depends on tumour size and location and surgeon experience.
key_toxicities: Bladder perforation is a potential complication, although preserving tumour architecture may reduce its risk.
monitoring: Assess completeness of resection and detrusor muscle in the specimen.

therapies_index.name: Piecemeal resection in fractions
approved_indications: Resection of bladder tumours in separate fractions.
therapies_index.administration: Remove the exophytic tumour, underlying bladder wall and resection margins separately.
monitoring: Assess the specimen for the tumour's vertical and horizontal extent.

therapies_index.name: monopolar resection
approved_indications: Technique for TURB.
key_toxicities: Obturator nerve stimulation can contribute to bladder perforation.

therapies_index.name: bipolar resection
approved_indications: Technique for TURB.

therapies_index.name: second TURB
approved_indications: Incomplete initial TURB or uncertainty about its completeness.
No detrusor muscle in the initial specimen, except in Ta LG/G1 tumours and primary CIS.
T1 tumours.
therapies_index.administration: When indicated, perform within two to six weeks after initial resection and resect the original tumour site.
monitoring: Record pathological findings, including residual tumour and any change in staging.

therapies_index.name: TURP
approved_indications: May accompany resection of incidentally found, small papillary bladder tumours that are not extensively multifocal.
May precede intravesical BCG when bladder preservation is considered for CIS in the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra.
therapies_index.administration: Resection of the prostate; in prostatic urethral CIS, it is followed by intravesical BCG.
key_toxicities: Capsular perforation precludes the proposed postoperative single chemotherapy instillation.

therapies_index.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
approved_indications: Discuss immediate RC for very high-risk NMIBC and as an option in high-risk disease.
Preferred treatment for BCG-unresponsive tumours.
An option for CIS and selected other categories of BCG failure.
key_toxicities: Operative complications, morbidity and impaired quality of life.

therapies_index.name: radical cystoprostatectomy
approved_indications: Immediate treatment when a bladder tumour invades the prostatic stroma.

therapies_index.name: office fulguration
approved_indications: Small recurrent low-grade Ta tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Performed on an outpatient basis.

therapies_index.name: laser vaporisation
approved_indications: Small papillary recurrences in patients with a history of small Ta LG/G1 tumours.
therapies_index.administration: May be performed on an outpatient basis.

therapies_index.name: laser photocoagulation
approved_indications: Studied as an outpatient alternative to TURB for small papillary recurrences.
therapies_index.administration: The cited trial used intravesical lidocaine in an outpatient setting.
key_toxicities: The cited trial reported a modest procedural pain score of 2.4.

therapies_index.name: Active Surveillance
approved_indications: An option for selected patients with presumed low-grade tumours instead of endoscopic ablation.
therapies_index.administration: Observation with intervention when clinically indicated; the cited approach considered changes in tumour size and multifocality as triggers.
monitoring: Surveil tumour size and multifocality.

therapies_index.name: chemoablation
therapies_index.mechanism: Intravesical chemotherapy is used to eliminate a tumour without preceding TURB.
approved_indications: An option for selected patients with presumed low-grade tumours instead of endoscopic ablation.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical drug schedules vary by agent and study.
monitoring: Assess complete response and subsequent recurrence.

therapies_index.name: post-operative irrigation
approved_indications: Continuous bladder irrigation with saline or water when a single postoperative chemotherapy instillation cannot be given.
therapies_index.administration: Continuous postoperative bladder irrigation; the optimal volume and duration have not been established.

therapies_index.name: intravesical chemotherapy
approved_indications: Adjuvant treatment after TURB according to recurrence and progression risk.
A first-line option for most intermediate-risk patients.
A bladder-preserving option for selected patients with BCG-unresponsive tumours who cannot undergo RC.
therapies_index.administration: Use an appropriate drug pH and reduce fluid intake before and during instillation to maintain drug concentration. Individual instillations should last a minimum of one, and up to two hours; further adjuvant treatment should not exceed one year.

therapies_index.name: single immediate instillation (SI)
therapies_index.mechanism: Post-TURB chemotherapy destroys circulating tumour cells and acts on residual cells at the resection site and small overlooked tumours.
approved_indications: After TURB in presumed low-risk tumours.
Small papillary recurrences presumed to be Ta LG/G1 and detected more than one year after previous TURB.
Immediate postoperative treatment in the EAU low-risk group.
therapies_index.administration: If used, give within 24 hours after TURB, preferably within the first two hours. Omit it with overt or suspected bladder perforation or bleeding that requires bladder irrigation.
key_toxicities: Severe complications have been reported with drug extravasation.

therapies_index.name: MMC
approved_indications: Studied as intravesical chemotherapy for postoperative instillation, repeated adjuvant treatment and chemoablation.
therapies_index.administration: An intravesical chemoablation trial used 40 mg/40 mL three times a week for two weeks. Another trial found a one-hour instillation more effective than a 30-minute instillation; preparations ≥ 1 mg/mL may not dissolve completely.

therapies_index.name: gemcitabine
approved_indications: Studied as a single postoperative intravesical instillation.
Used sequentially with docetaxel as an emerging bladder-preserving approach after BCG failure.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation; a dose is not specified.

therapies_index.name: epirubicin
approved_indications: Studied as a single postoperative intravesical instillation and in further intravesical treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation; a regimen is not specified.

therapies_index.name: pirarubicin
approved_indications: Studied as a single postoperative intravesical instillation.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation; a dose is not specified.

therapies_index.name: apaziquone
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as a bioreductive prodrug similar to MMC.
approved_indications: Investigated as a single postoperative intravesical instillation; two trials found no overall effect, although a post-hoc analysis suggested less recurrence when given within 90 minutes after TURB.
therapies_index.administration: Investigated after TURB, including administration within 90 minutes.

therapies_index.name: UGN-102
therapies_index.mechanism: A mitomycin-containing reverse thermal gel used for chemoablation.
approved_indications: Investigated in low-grade intermediate-risk NMIBC and recurrent low-grade intermediate-risk NMIBC.
therapies_index.administration: In the cited trials, administered once weekly for six weeks, with or without subsequent TURB.
monitoring: Assess complete response at three months.

therapies_index.name: cytosine arabinoside
approved_indications: Investigated as an addition to intravesical MMC to reduce recurrence.

therapies_index.name: peroral sodium bicarbonate
approved_indications: Investigated as part of measures to optimise intravesical MMC administration.
therapies_index.administration: Taken orally as part of a studied combination that also used a higher MMC dose and restricted drinking.

therapies_index.name: BCG
approved_indications: Intravesical treatment for intermediate-risk NMIBC as an alternative to chemotherapy.
Intravesical treatment for high-risk NMIBC and an option for selected very high-risk patients.
Treatment of CIS, including CIS in the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra when bladder preservation is considered.
An option for selected recurrences after intravesical chemotherapy or earlier BCG that do not meet BCG-unresponsive criteria.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical induction comprises six weekly instillations. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at 3, 6 and 12 months, with additional cycles at 18, 24, 30 and 36 months when indicated. Do not instil during the first two weeks after TURB, with visible haematuria, after traumatic catheterisation or with symptomatic urinary tract infection.
key_toxicities: Malaise, fever, arthralgia or arthritis, and allergic reactions.
BCG infection and sepsis; serious side effects occur in < 5% of patients.
monitoring: Assess local and systemic symptoms and their severity.
Investigate persistent high-grade fever (> 38.5°C for > 48 h) immediately.
Assess response and recurrence during treatment and follow-up.

therapies_index.name: intravesical BCG for one to three years
approved_indications: Indicated at full dose for high-risk tumours.
An option at full dose for selected very high-risk patients, particularly when RC is declined or unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: Induction followed by three-weekly maintenance instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months, according to treatment duration.
key_toxicities: BCG-related local and systemic side effects.
monitoring: Assess tolerability and response during maintenance.

therapies_index.name: one-year full-dose BCG treatment
approved_indications: An alternative to chemotherapy for intermediate-risk NMIBC.
therapies_index.administration: Induction followed by three-weekly instillations at 3, 6 and 12 months.
key_toxicities: BCG-related local and systemic side effects.
monitoring: Assess response and tolerability.

therapies_index.name: MMC and microwave-induced hyperthermia
therapies_index.mechanism: Microwave-induced heating increases the temperature of instilled MMC.
approved_indications: Investigated for intermediate- and high-risk NMIBC and after BCG failure.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical MMC with microwave-induced hyperthermia; a cited comparative trial used one year of treatment.
monitoring: Assess disease recurrence.

therapies_index.name: HIVEC
approved_indications: Investigated in intermediate-risk NMIBC; cited trials did not establish superiority over standard or normothermic intravesical chemotherapy.
therapies_index.administration: A cited trial evaluated four-month adjuvant hyperthermic MMC using the COMBAT system.
key_toxicities: A cited trial reported more treatment discontinuation than with standard adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy.
monitoring: Assess treatment completion and disease-free survival.

therapies_index.name: HIVEC™ MMC
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines intravesical MMC with conductive chemohyperthermia.
approved_indications: Investigated in high-risk NMIBC; the cited pilot trial requires confirmation.
monitoring: Assess recurrence-free survival.

therapies_index.name: EMDA
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses electromotive administration to deliver intravesical chemotherapy.
approved_indications: Investigated for intravesical MMC administration, including treatment combined sequentially with BCG.
therapies_index.administration: Electromotive intravesical drug administration.

therapies_index.name: EMDA-MMC
therapies_index.mechanism: Delivers intravesical MMC by electromotive administration.
approved_indications: Investigated in patients with BCG-refractory HG NMIBC.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical MMC delivered by EMDA; a schedule is not specified.
monitoring: Assess disease-free status.

therapies_index.name: BCG and MMC with EMDA
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines intravesical BCG with electromotive administration of MMC.
approved_indications: Investigated in high-risk tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Sequential intravesical treatment; a detailed schedule is not specified.
monitoring: Assess recurrence and progression.

therapies_index.name: MMC and BCG
approved_indications: Investigated as combined intravesical treatment for NMIBC.
therapies_index.administration: In one cited trial, an MMC instillation preceded each BCG instillation by a day.
key_toxicities: The cited comparison found greater toxicity than with BCG alone.
monitoring: Assess recurrence and treatment toxicity.

therapies_index.name: BCG and IFN-2α
approved_indications: Investigated in NMIBC; a cited meta-analysis did not show a clear difference in recurrence or progression compared with BCG alone.

therapies_index.name: IFN-2α
approved_indications: Investigated in combination with BCG or in an alternating intravesical schedule.

therapies_index.name: epirubicin and INF
approved_indications: Investigated for prevention of NMIBC recurrence; the cited trial found it inferior to BCG monotherapy.
therapies_index.administration: The cited trial evaluated treatment for up to two years.
monitoring: Assess recurrence.

therapies_index.name: gemcitabine and docetaxel
approved_indications: An emerging bladder-preserving approach after BCG failure, including BCG-unresponsive disease when RC is infeasible or declined; further prospective evaluation is awaited.
Also reported in BCG-naïve high-risk patients.
therapies_index.administration: Sequential intravesical instillations; a schedule is not specified.
monitoring: Assess treatment response and recurrence.

therapies_index.name: docetaxel
approved_indications: Reported in sequential intravesical combinations with gemcitabine or valrubicin.
therapies_index.administration: Sequential intravesical instillation; a dose is not specified.

therapies_index.name: valrubicin and docetaxel
approved_indications: Suggested as a sequential intravesical chemotherapy combination.
therapies_index.administration: Sequential intravesical instillations; a schedule is not specified.

therapies_index.name: valrubicin
approved_indications: Suggested in a sequential intravesical combination with docetaxel.

therapies_index.name: pembrolizumab
approved_indications: FDA approval is reported for the studied population with BCG-unresponsive CIS alone or concomitant with papillary tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Systemic administration; a schedule is not specified.
monitoring: Assess complete response and its durability.

therapies_index.name: Atezolizumab
approved_indications: Investigated in BCG-unresponsive CIS and papillary-only Ta/T1 disease.
therapies_index.administration: Systemic administration; a schedule is not specified.
monitoring: Assess response and event-free survival.

therapies_index.name: Nadofaragene firadenovec
approved_indications: FDA approval is reported for BCG-unresponsive CIS.
monitoring: Assess complete response and whether an initial response persists at one year.

therapies_index.name: Nagopendekin alfa-inbakicept (NAI)
approved_indications: Investigated in BCG-unresponsive HG NMIBC, including CIS and Ta/T1 disease.
monitoring: Assess complete response in CIS and disease-free survival in Ta/T1 disease.

therapies_index.name: Erdafitinib
approved_indications: Investigated in recurrent Ta/T1 HG disease after BCG in patients with selected FGFR alterations who refused or were unfit for radical cystectomy.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration; a dose is not specified.
monitoring: Assess recurrence-free survival.

therapies_index.name: PDD
therapies_index.mechanism: Blue-light visualisation after intravesical administration of ALA or HAL aids identification of malignant lesions.
approved_indications: An available method to improve tumour visualisation during TURB or guide biopsies.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical ALA or HAL precedes blue-light examination.
key_toxicities: Inflammation, recent TURB and the first three months after BCG can cause false-positive findings.

therapies_index.name: 5-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA)
approved_indications: Used for PDD-assisted bladder tumour visualisation.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation before blue-light examination.

therapies_index.name: hexaminolaevulinic acid (HAL)
approved_indications: Used for PDD-assisted bladder tumour visualisation.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical instillation before blue-light examination.

therapies_index.name: Thulium-YAG laser
approved_indications: A potential alternative for fractionated resection and an option for en-bloc resection of selected exophytic tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic laser resection.

therapies_index.name: Holmium-YAG
approved_indications: An option for en-bloc resection of selected exophytic tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic laser resection.

therapies_index.name: KTP-Green Light lasers
approved_indications: An option for en-bloc resection of selected exophytic tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Endoscopic laser resection.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
approved_indications: Used during outpatient laser photocoagulation in the cited trial.
therapies_index.administration: Intravesical administration in the cited trial.

therapies_index.name: Phenazopyridine
approved_indications: An option for cystitis symptoms associated with intravesical BCG.
monitoring: Assess whether symptoms improve or persist.

therapies_index.name: propantheline bromide
approved_indications: An option for cystitis symptoms associated with intravesical BCG.
monitoring: Assess whether symptoms improve or persist.

therapies_index.name: NSAIDs
approved_indications: An option for BCG-associated cystitis symptoms, arthralgia or reactive arthritis.
monitoring: Assess symptom response.

therapies_index.name: quinolones
approved_indications: A cautious option for BCG-related side effects.
Included among options for persistent cystitis symptoms, symptomatic granulomatous prostatitis, epididymo-orchitis and severe BCG infection.
therapies_index.administration: High doses are listed among options for severe BCG infection; other doses are not specified.
key_toxicities: The guide notes European restrictions arising from the side-effect profile of quinolones and fluoroquinolones.
monitoring: Assess symptom response and obtain urine culture where indicated.

therapies_index.name: levofloxacin
approved_indications: Studied to reduce side effects accompanying BCG instillations; the cited trial did not improve maintenance completion or severe BCG-related adverse events.
therapies_index.administration: The cited trial used two doses at six and twelve hours after first voiding with each BCG instillation.
key_toxicities: The guide notes restrictions arising from the side-effect profile of quinolones and fluoroquinolones.
monitoring: Assess local and systemic BCG-related side effects.

therapies_index.name: isoniazid
approved_indications: Listed for granulomatous prostatitis when quinolones are ineffective and for severe BCG infection.
Listed as an option with rifampicin for persistent allergic symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: For granulomatous prostatitis, 300 mg/day with rifampicin for three months; a dose is not specified for other uses.

therapies_index.name: rifampicin
approved_indications: Listed for granulomatous prostatitis when quinolones are ineffective and for severe BCG infection.
Listed with isoniazid as an option for persistent allergic symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: For granulomatous prostatitis, 600 mg/day with isoniazid for three months; a dose is not specified for other uses.

therapies_index.name: ethambutol
approved_indications: Listed as part of treatment for severe BCG infection.
therapies_index.administration: 1.2 g daily for six months in the listed severe-infection regimen.

therapies_index.name: isoniazid, rifampicin, and ethambutol
approved_indications: A listed treatment option for severe BCG infection.
therapies_index.administration: The guide lists ethambutol 1.2 g daily for six months with isoniazid and rifampicin.
monitoring: Assess infection symptoms.

therapies_index.name: corticosteroids
approved_indications: An option for persistent BCG-related cystitis symptoms or arthritis with inadequate response to earlier treatment.
Listed for severe BCG infection.
therapies_index.administration: For severe BCG infection, start high doses early and continue while symptoms persist.
monitoring: Assess whether symptoms persist.

therapies_index.name: antipyretics
approved_indications: An option for general malaise and fever after BCG.
monitoring: Assess fever, which generally resolves within 48 hours.

therapies_index.name: Antihistamines
approved_indications: An option for allergic reactions associated with BCG.
monitoring: Delay BCG therapy until the reaction resolves.

therapies_index.name: Orchidectomy
approved_indications: BCG-associated epididymo-orchitis with an abscess or no response to treatment.

conditions.name: Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer (TaT1 and CIS)
conditions.description: For treatment purposes, this group comprises urothelial tumours confined to the mucosa, tumours invading the lamina propria, and intra-epithelial high-grade carcinoma in situ. Each tumour still requires individual characterisation by stage, grade and other pathological features.
conditions.epidemiology: Approximately 75% of patients with bladder cancer present with disease confined to the mucosa or submucosa; the proportion is higher among patients aged < 40 years. Worldwide, bladder cancer is the seventh most commonly diagnosed cancer in men and the tenth when both sexes are considered. Age-standardised incidence per 100,000 person/years is 9.5 in men and 2.4 in women worldwide, and 20 and 4.6, respectively, in the European Union. Long survival in many patients with TaT1 and CIS contributes to high disease prevalence.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Haematuria is the most frequent finding. Visible haematuria is associated with a higher stage at diagnosis than nonvisible haematuria. Lower urinary tract symptoms, particularly irritative voiding symptoms, can raise suspicion of CIS.

subtypes.name: TaT1 tumours
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Papillary tumours are distinguished by whether they remain within the mucosa or invade the lamina propria.

subtypes.name: Carcinoma in situ
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A flat, intra-epithelial HG tumour that can occur with or without a papillary tumour.

subtypes.name: Pure UC
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Accounts for more than 90% of UC cases.

subtypes.name: UC with partial (squamous-glandular or trophoblastic) divergent differentiation
UC with micropapillary divergent differentiation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Micropapillary histology is among the subtypes associated with greater risks of recurrence and progression.

subtypes.name: UC with large nested divergent differentiation
UC with plasmacytoid divergent differentiation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Plasmacytoid histology is among the subtypes associated with greater risks of recurrence and progression.

subtypes.name: UC with giant cell, diffuse, undifferentiated divergent differentiation
UC with sarcomatoid divergent differentiation
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Sarcomatoid histology is among the subtypes associated with greater risks of recurrence and progression.

subtypes.name: UCs with partial NE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The percentage of neuroendocrine differentiation should be reported.

subtypes.name: pure neuroendocrine carcinoma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes small and large cell neuroendocrine carcinomas; neuroendocrine histology is among the subtypes associated with greater risks of recurrence and progression.

subtypes.name: BCG-unresponsive tumour
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes BCG-refractory tumours and specified early HG recurrences after adequate BCG exposure.

subtypes.name: BCG-exposed tumour
subtypes.distinguishing_features: HG recurrence after BCG that does not fulfil the criteria for BCG-unresponsive disease.

diagnostic_workup.test: Focused patient history and urological examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess haematuria, urinary symptoms and relevant clinical findings.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The examination itself does not reveal NMIBC.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate renal masses, hydronephrosis and intraluminal bladder masses.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment of haematuria; it may complement physical examination.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It cannot exclude every cause of haematuria or reliably rule out UTUC and cannot replace CT urography.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify urinary tract papillary tumours, filling defects or hydronephrosis and assess the upper tract.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Selected patients after detection of a bladder tumour, including those with a trigonal, multiple or high-risk tumour; upper tract assessment during indicated follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Baseline use in every patient with a detected bladder tumour is of uncertain necessity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Image the urinary tract.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: An alternative when CT is unavailable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CT urography supplies more information, particularly for muscle-invasive bladder tumours and UTUC.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide additional information on local bladder cancer stage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If used for local staging, before TURB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A VI-RADS score of > 4 had pooled weighted sensitivity of 0.78 and specificity of 0.94 for predicting MIBC in a systematic review. Imaging alone cannot establish CIS.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Examine the bladder for a papillary tumour or suspicious mucosa and record tumour location, size, number and appearance.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Symptoms suggestive of bladder cancer and surveillance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Diagnosis of a papillary tumour also requires histological assessment of sampled tissue. Cytology and other non-invasive tests cannot replace cystoscopy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect exfoliated malignant cells, particularly from HG/G3 tumours, as an adjunct to cystoscopy.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment and surveillance when appropriate to risk; investigate a suspicious result again.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reported sensitivity is 84% for HG and G3 tumours, 16% for LG/G1 tumours and 28–100% for CIS. Positive voided cytology can indicate UC anywhere in the urinary tract, whereas a negative result does not exclude UC. The Paris System 2nd Edn. supplies reporting categories.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide adjunctive information about detection or recurrence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Investigated in primary detection and surveillance, but not accepted for routine diagnosis or follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Sensitivity is generally higher and specificity lower than for urinary cytology. Benign conditions and previous BCG instillations can affect results; no urinary marker routinely replaces cystoscopy or reduces its frequency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Remove visible lesions and establish pathological diagnosis, stage and grade.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected bladder tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The pathology report should specify stage, grade, LVI, UC subtypes, CIS and the presence of detrusor muscle. Missing detrusor muscle is associated with significantly greater risks of residual disease and understaging, except in Ta LG/G1 tumours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Histologically assess suspicious urothelium or investigate positive cytology despite normal-looking bladder mucosa.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Abnormal-appearing mucosa; mapping biopsies or PDD-guided biopsies if cytology is positive and the mucosa appears normal.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Representative mapping samples come from the trigone, dome, and right, left, anterior and posterior walls.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify tumour or CIS in the prostatic urethra.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour, visible prostatic urethral abnormality, bladder neck tumour, suspected bladder CIS or T1 disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Improve visualisation for biopsy and resection, particularly of CIS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During TURB if available, or to target indicated biopsies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A meta-analysis reported patient-level sensitivity of 92% versus 71% with WL and biopsy-level sensitivity of 93% versus 65%; specificity was 63% versus 81%. Inflammation, recent TURB and the first three months after BCG can cause false-positive findings.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Improve visual contrast for tumour detection during cystoscopy, biopsy or resection.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During TURB if available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Improved detection has been reported, but overall recurrence results from two RCTs were negative.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Enhance endoscopic images.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Evidence for improved diagnostic accuracy is limited.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Remove residual disease, reassess the original site for accurate staging and obtain missing clinical information.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Incomplete initial TURB or uncertainty about completeness; absent detrusor muscle except in Ta LG/G1 tumours and primary CIS; or T1 tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: When indicated, it should include the original tumour site and take place within two to six weeks of initial resection.

diagnostic_workup.test: CT urography and prostatic urethral biopsy
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate extravesical disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour, including during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The investigation specifically addresses UTUC and a prostatic urethral tumour, alongside bladder biopsies to assess for CIS.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Its presence in a TURB specimen is associated with more pathological upstaging and a worse prognosis; patients with LVI are placed in the very high-risk group.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Present in an adequate resection specimen except where sampling is not required for Ta LG/G1 tumours.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Absence is associated with significantly more residual disease, early recurrence and understaging.
Concomitant CIS contributes to progression-risk classification and increases recurrence and progression risk in TaT1 tumours.

genetic_molecular.clinical_significance: With negative cystoscopy and upper tract assessment, a positive result may identify patients more likely to develop recurrence and possibly progression.
With negative cystoscopy and upper tract assessment, a positive result may identify patients more likely to develop recurrence and possibly progression.
A positive urine result despite negative cystoscopy and upper tract assessment may identify patients more likely to recur and possibly progress.
A positive result despite negative cystoscopy and upper tract assessment may identify patients more likely to recur and possibly progress.

No primary tumour is evident.
Papillary carcinoma without invasion.
Flat carcinoma in situ.
