staging.additional_rules: When lamina propria sampling is adequate, T1 can be substaged using micrometric T1e and T1m or histo-anatomic T1a and T1b principles; the optimal method is undetermined. Histological grading uses WHO 2004/2016/2022 categories PUNLMP, LG and HG and/or WHO 1973 categories G1, G2 and G3. The WHO 2022 classification considers UC subtypes HG and classifies tumours containing more than 5% HG as HG.

prognostic_tools.name: 2006 EORTC scoring model
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Estimates recurrence and progression probabilities at one and five years, principally from patients treated with intravesical chemotherapy. It is recommended for predicting individual recurrence risk in patients not treated with BCG.

prognostic_tools.name: The model for patients with Ta G1/G2 (WHO 1973) tumours treated with chemotherapy

risk_groups.criteria: Stratification uses the listed clinical and treatment factors; individual group thresholds are not specified.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Stratifies recurrence risk in chemotherapy-treated Ta G1/G2 tumours.

prognostic_tools.name: CUETO scoring model
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Predicts recurrence and progression after 12 doses of intravesical BCG over five to six months. Its calculated recurrence risk is lower than in the EORTC tables; progression probability is lower only for high-risk patients.

prognostic_tools.name: 2016 EORTC scoring model
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Developed for patients without CIS receiving one to three years of maintenance BCG. Prior recurrence and tumour number chiefly predict recurrence; stage and grade chiefly predict progression and disease-specific survival; age and grade chiefly predict OS. T1 G3 patients had one- and five-year progression rates of 11.4% and 19.8%, respectively.

prognostic_tools.name: EAU NMIBC 2021 scoring model

risk_groups.criteria: Primary single TaT1 LG/G1 tumour < 3 cm without CIS at age ≤ 70 years; or primary Ta LG/G1 tumour without CIS and at most ONE additional clinical risk factor. Additional factors are age > 70, multiple papillary tumours and tumour diameter > 3 cm.
Patients without CIS who do not meet low-, high- or very high-risk criteria.

T1 HG/G3 without CIS or CIS, unless very high-risk criteria apply; alternatively, Ta LG/G2 or T1G1 without CIS plus all 3 additional factors, Ta HG/G3 or T1 LG without CIS plus at least 2 factors, or T1G2 without CIS plus at least 1 factor.

Ta HG/G3 with CIS and all 3 additional factors; T1G2 with CIS and at least 2; T1 HG/G3 with CIS and at least 1; or T1 HG/G3 without CIS and all 3. CIS in the prostatic urethra, UC subtypes or LVI also warrant inclusion on the basis of literature data.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Predicts progression rather than recurrence. The tabulated probabilities concern primary patients not immediately given adjuvant BCG after TURB and exclude UC subtypes, LVI, prostatic urethral CIS, primary CIS and recurrent tumours. Either grading system can assign a risk group; when both are available, the Panel recommends WHO 1973 because of its better prognostic value. Recurrent tumours are assigned to intermediate-, high- or very high-risk groups according to other prognostic factors.

prognostic_tools.name: IBCG

risk_groups.criteria: No factors in the refined intermediate-risk substratification model.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: In a validation study, one-year progression risk resembled that of the EAU2021 low-risk group.

risk_groups.criteria: At least 3 factors in the refined intermediate-risk substratification model.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: In a validation study, one-year progression risk aligned with that of the EAU2021 high-risk group.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: A three-tier intermediate-risk substratification model refined in 2022; longer follow-up and external validation remain necessary.

follow_up.schedule: All patients with TaT1 tumours or CIS should have their first cystoscopy three months after TURB. Later frequency and duration depend on risk group: low risk, at 3 and 12 months then annually for 5 years; intermediate risk excluding HG/G3, at 3 months then every 6 months for 2 years and annually to 10 years; high and very high risk treated conservatively, every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months up to 5 years, then annually for life. Intermediate-risk HG/G3 follows the high-risk schedule.
recommended_tests: Urinary cytology alongside cystoscopy for high- and very high-risk disease
CT annually up to 5 years, then CT every 2 years up to 10 years for high- and very high-risk disease
CT urography to investigate indicated upper tract concerns
Bladder biopsies and investigation of extravesical sites when cytology is positive without a visible bladder tumour
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Repeated hospital visits, TURB, surveillance cystoscopy and intravesical instillations can substantially affect QoL. Follow-up recommendations are mainly supported by retrospective evidence, and randomised evidence on safely reducing cystoscopy frequency is lacking.

conditions.name: TaT1 tumours
conditions.description: This designation encompasses mucosa-confined Ta tumours and T1 tumours that invade the lamina propria. Stage and grade influence decisions about additional treatment and surveillance.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Haematuria is the most common finding in NMIBC.

subtypes.name: Ta LG/G1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Low-grade, non-invasive papillary disease; small recurrences can be considered for office fulguration or, in selected patients, surveillance or chemoablation.

subtypes.name: T1 HG/G3
subtypes.distinguishing_features: High-grade lamina propria-invasive disease; the presence of CIS and other risk factors can place it in the very high-risk group.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cystoscopy with cold-cup biopsy or TURB
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a papillary lesion and obtain tissue for diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspected papillary bladder tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Histology establishes the diagnosis and pathological classification.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Completely remove visible lesions and determine stage and grade.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial management of suspected TaT1 tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Record tumour number, size, architecture, location, resection completeness and whether detrusor muscle was sampled.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and remove residual tumour and reassess stage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Incomplete or questionably complete first resection, absent detrusor muscle except in Ta LG/G1, or T1 tumour.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: When indicated, repeat resection includes the original site within two to six weeks.

pathology_markers.expected_result: Present in the resection specimen except where not required for Ta LG/G1.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Absence is associated with significantly greater risks of residual disease, early recurrence and understaging.
Its presence is associated with pathological upstaging and worse prognosis.

definitions.description: A papillary carcinoma without invasion.
The tumour invades subepithelial connective tissue.

staging.additional_rules: T1 substaging can follow micrometric T1e and T1m or histo-anatomic T1a and T1b principles when the lamina propria is adequately sampled.

follow_up.schedule: First cystoscopy three months after TURB; later surveillance follows the assigned risk group.
recommended_tests: Urinary cytology for high- and very high-risk disease
Upper tract imaging for high- and very high-risk disease

conditions.name: Carcinoma in situ
conditions.description: An intra-epithelial, HG, non-invasive UC that can occur in the bladder, UUT, prostatic ducts or prostatic urethra. It cannot be cured by endoscopic treatment alone.
conditions.epidemiology: Without treatment, approximately 54% of patients with CIS progress to muscle-invasive disease. Approximately 10 to 20% of complete responders to intravesical treatment eventually progress, compared with 66% of nonresponders.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Irritative voiding symptoms can prompt suspicion. At cystoscopy, CIS can resemble a reddish, velvet-like inflammatory area or be invisible.

subtypes.name: Primary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Isolated CIS without earlier CIS and without previous or simultaneous papillary tumours.

subtypes.name: Secondary
subtypes.distinguishing_features: CIS found during surveillance after a previous non-CIS tumour.

subtypes.name: Concurrent
subtypes.distinguishing_features: CIS occurring together with another bladder urothelial tumour.

subtypes.name: CIS in the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Epithelial involvement must be distinguished from prostatic duct involvement and invasion of prostatic stroma.

subtypes.name: CIS in the prostatic ducts
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document describes limited treatment evidence from small BCG-treated series.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Raise suspicion of CIS.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Initial assessment or surveillance, including evaluation of positive urine cytology.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cystoscopy can miss CIS or mistake it for inflammation; cytology alone does not establish the diagnosis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm CIS histologically.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suspicious mucosa or positive cytology with normal-looking mucosa.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Mapping samples include the trigone, dome, and right, left, anterior and posterior bladder walls.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Target suspicious mucosa for histological assessment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Where equipment is available, particularly with positive cytology and no visible lesion.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: PDD improves detection, particularly of CIS, but cannot rule out prostatic involvement.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify prostatic urethral or duct involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour, suspected bladder CIS or other specified clinical indications.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate UUT involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Positive cytology without a visible bladder tumour or indicated surveillance for extravesical recurrence.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CT urography, IVU, US and MRI cannot establish CIS without histology.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: CIS is defined as a high-grade intra-epithelial tumour.

definitions.description: Flat carcinoma in situ.
In bladder tumours, invasion of the prostatic stroma is classified separately from epithelial or ductal CIS.

staging.additional_rules: CIS of the epithelial lining or ducts of the prostatic urethra must be distinguished from invasion of prostatic stroma.

follow_up.schedule: Cystoscopy is required three months after TURB. Subsequent surveillance reflects the patient's risk group; conservatively treated high- and very high-risk patients undergo cystoscopy and cytology every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months until 5 years, then annually for life.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Response to intravesical BCG or chemotherapy is an important prognostic factor for subsequent progression and bladder cancer death.

conditions.name: BCG-unresponsive tumour
conditions.description: A category of HG disease after BCG for which further BCG is unlikely to provide benefit. It includes BCG-refractory tumours and Ta/T1 HG recurrence within 6 months, or CIS within 12 months, after completion of adequate BCG exposure.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Persistent or recurrent HG bladder disease during or after BCG treatment.

subtypes.name: BCG-refractory tumour
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Includes T1 HG/G3 at 3 months; Ta HG/G3 after 3 months and/or at 6 months after re-induction or first maintenance; CIS without a concomitant papillary tumour present at 3 months and persisting at 6 months after re-induction or first maintenance; or an HG tumour arising during BCG maintenance.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cystoscopy, urinary cytology and histological assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify persistent or recurrent HG tumour and determine whether CIS is present.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Assessment during or after intravesical BCG.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Non-HG recurrence after BCG does not constitute BCG failure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine adequacy of exposure and the interval from treatment to recurrence.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Classification of HG recurrence after BCG.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Adequate BCG requires at least five of six initial induction doses plus at least two out of six doses of a second induction course or two out of three maintenance doses.

definitions.description: A non-invasive papillary HG recurrence can qualify when it occurs within the specified interval after adequate BCG.
An HG lamina propria-invasive recurrence can qualify when it occurs within the specified interval after adequate BCG.
CIS can qualify when it occurs within 12 months after adequate BCG.

staging.additional_rules: The definition also encompasses BCG-refractory disease. MIBC detected during follow-up requires recognition as muscle-invasive disease rather than a non-muscle-invasive recurrence.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up after conservative treatment depends on the high- or very high-risk surveillance schedule: cystoscopy and urinary cytology every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months up to 5 years, and annually thereafter for life.
recommended_tests: Upper tract imaging according to risk
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline regards treatments other than RC as oncologically inferior for this category.

conditions.name: BCG-exposed tumour
conditions.description: HG recurrence after BCG that does not meet the criteria for BCG-unresponsive disease. This category includes specified persistence after induction and delayed relapse.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Persistent or recurrent Ta HG/G3, T1 HG or CIS detected during follow-up after BCG.

subtypes.name: BCG-resistant
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Persistent or recurrent Ta HG and/or CIS at three months after at least five of six induction BCG doses; exposure is inadequate under the definition of adequate BCG.

subtypes.name: Delayed relapse after inadequate BCG
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Ta/T1 HG or CIS recurring between 6 and 24 months in a patient disease-free at three months who received no more than an induction course.

subtypes.name: Delayed relapse after adequate BCG
subtypes.distinguishing_features: HG recurrence after an initial disease-free response to adequate BCG, outside the BCG-unresponsive interval of > 6 months for Ta/T1 or > 12 months for CIS, up to 24 months.

diagnostic_workup.test: Cystoscopy, urinary cytology and histological assessment
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish whether recurrent disease is HG and identify its stage or CIS status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Surveillance after BCG.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: LG recurrence after BCG is not classified as BCG failure.

diagnostic_workup.test: Review of BCG exposure and recurrence timing
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Distinguish BCG-exposed disease from BCG-unresponsive disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: HG persistence or recurrence following BCG.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Classification depends on previous induction or maintenance doses and the time elapsed since BCG.

definitions.description: A non-invasive papillary HG recurrence can fall within this category.
A lamina propria-invasive HG recurrence can fall within delayed-relapse categories.
CIS can fall within this category according to its timing and previous BCG exposure.

staging.additional_rules: The BCG-exposed classification concerns HG disease that falls outside the BCG-unresponsive definition.

follow_up.schedule: Surveillance follows the applicable high-risk schedule if disease is managed conservatively.
recommended_tests: Upper tract imaging according to risk

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients suspected of having bladder cancer.
decision_rules: Use TURB to establish the pathological diagnosis and stage and to remove every visible lesion.
Choose en-bloc or fractioned resection according to tumour size and location and the surgeon’s experience.
Obtain detrusor muscle for assessment of resection quality, except in Ta LG/G1 tumours.

recommended_regimens.name: TURB
recommended_regimens.summary: Perform TURB as the diagnostic and initial treatment procedure, followed by pathological examination. Inspect the urethra and bladder, perform indicated biopsies, resect the tumour, and document the operative findings and specimens.

recommended_regimens.name: en-bloc resection
recommended_regimens.summary: An accepted method of complete tumour removal in selected lesions.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A multicentre RCT reported detrusor muscle in 80.7 with en-bloc resection versus 71.1 with conventional TURB. Another RCT in tumours < 3 cm reported a reduction in one-year recurrence from 38.1% to 28.5%; other RCTs did not show a difference in time to recurrence.

recommended_regimens.name: resection in fractions
recommended_regimens.summary: Resect the exophytic tumour, underlying bladder wall and resection margins separately to assess tumour extent.

response_assessment.method: Visual assessment of completeness and pathological examination of the submitted specimens
response_assessment.interpretation: Document residual tumour, clinical impression of grade and stage, detrusor muscle sampling and any complications.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Minimise cauterisation to preserve tissue quality. Send biopsy and fractioned-resection specimens in separately labelled containers; submit the tumour base separately, particularly for large or multifocal tumours or when en-bloc resection is not feasible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with an incomplete initial TURB or uncertainty about completeness; patients whose initial specimen lacks detrusor muscle, except those with Ta LG/G1 tumours or primary CIS; and patients with T1 tumours.
decision_rules: Perform another TURB when any specified indication is present, including when completion of the initial resection is required.
Resect the original tumour site again and record the pathological findings.

recommended_regimens.name: second TURB
recommended_regimens.summary: Remove residual disease and reassess the original resection site for accurate staging.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic review of 8,409 patients with Ta or T1 HG UC reported 51% persistence and 8% under-staging in T1 tumours. Another review reported pooled T1 residual-disease and upstaging rates of 31.4% and 2.8%, respectively. In a review of 81 studies, repeat TURB was associated with better RFS (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62-0.97) and OS (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.810.93), without a difference in PFS or CSS.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within two to six weeks after the initial resection when indicated

response_assessment.method: Pathological assessment of the primary tumour site
response_assessment.interpretation: Record residual tumour and any change in stage; these findings also reflect the effectiveness of the initial TURB.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation to perform an indicated second TURB is Strong; the recommendation specifying its timing and inclusion of the primary tumour site is Weak. For T1 tumours, residual T1 disease at second TURB is an unfavourable prognostic finding.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with tumours presumed to be low risk, or a small papillary recurrence presumed to be Ta LG/G1 more than one year after a previous TURB.
decision_rules: Offer one immediate intravesical chemotherapy instillation after TURB.
Do not give the immediate instillation when bladder perforation is apparent or suspected, or bleeding requires bladder irrigation.

recommended_regimens.name: single immediate instillation of intravesical chemotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Give one postoperative instillation to reduce recurrence after TURB. When administered, deliver it within 24 hours, preferably as soon as possible.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 2,278 eligible patients found a 14% reduction in five-year recurrence, from 59% to 45%. Benefit was reported for patients with primary tumours, patients with intermediate-risk recurrent tumours and a prior recurrence rate of < 1 recurrence/year, and patients with a 2006 EORTC recurrence score < 5.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: One instillation within 24 hours after TURB; preferably within the first two hours

alternative_regimens.name: mitomycin C (MMC)
alternative_regimens.summary: One of the agents reported to lower intravesical recurrence when used for the single instillation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection among individual agents is not supported by randomised head-to-head comparisons.

alternative_regimens.name: epirubicin
alternative_regimens.summary: One of the agents reported to lower intravesical recurrence when used for the single instillation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection among individual agents is not supported by randomised head-to-head comparisons.

alternative_regimens.name: pirarubicin
alternative_regimens.summary: One of the agents reported to lower intravesical recurrence when used for the single instillation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selection among individual agents is not supported by randomised head-to-head comparisons.

alternative_regimens.name: gemcitabine
alternative_regimens.summary: One instillation reduced intravesical recurrence; an RCT comparing it with saline reported remarkably low toxicity.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An available agent for the single postoperative instillation.

alternative_regimens.name: continuous saline or water bladder irrigation
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer postoperative continuous irrigation instead of the single chemotherapy instillation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient cannot receive the single chemotherapy instillation.

not_recommended.name: single immediate instillation of intravesical chemotherapy
not_recommended.reason: Omit it with overt or suspected bladder perforation or bleeding that requires bladder irrigation.

response_assessment.interpretation: The first post-TURB examination provides prognostic information about recurrence and progression.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation to give an indicated instillation within 24 hours has a Weak strength rating. Single instillation alone was not effective for a 2006 EORTC recurrence score > 5 and/or a prior recurrence rate of > 1 recurrence per year.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients in the low-risk group.
decision_rules: After TURB, use a single postoperative intravesical chemotherapy instillation as sufficient adjuvant treatment for this risk group.

recommended_regimens.name: single immediate instillation of intravesical chemotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Give one immediate instillation after TURB to lower recurrence risk.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: An individual-patient-data meta-analysis reported five-year recurrence of 45% after single instillation versus 59% without it, a reduction of 14% in its eligible study population.

alternative_regimens.name: continuous saline or water bladder irrigation
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer continuous postoperative bladder irrigation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The single chemotherapy instillation cannot be administered.

not_recommended.name: single immediate instillation of intravesical chemotherapy
not_recommended.reason: Omit it if bladder perforation is overt or suspected, or bleeding requires bladder irrigation.

response_assessment.timepoint: At 3 and 12 months, then annually for 5 years if the first examination is negative
response_assessment.interpretation: Follow-up is guided by recurrence findings; discontinuing cystoscopy or replacing it with a less invasive approach after five years should be considered.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Low-risk disease has a negligible risk of progression according to the guideline.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients in the intermediate-risk group.
decision_rules: Select further treatment using the patient’s recurrence and progression risks and the efficacy and adverse effects of each option.
Chemotherapy is a reasonable initial option for most patients; a one-year full-dose BCG course is an alternative.
Offer a single immediate chemotherapy instillation for a small papillary recurrence detected more than one year after previous TURB.

recommended_regimens.name: intravesical chemotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use induction chemotherapy as a reasonable first-line approach for most intermediate-risk patients, with or without maintenance. Repeated instillations improve RFS in this group.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A meta-analysis of 3,703 patients in 11 RCTs reported a 44% reduction in the odds of recurrence at one year versus TURB alone, corresponding to an absolute difference of 13–14% in the proportion with recurrence.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Induction with or without maintenance; do not exceed one year

alternative_regimens.name: BCG
alternative_regimens.summary: Full-dose induction followed by three-weekly maintenance instillations is an alternative to chemotherapy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to individual recurrence and progression risks and the relative efficacy and side effects of chemotherapy and BCG; treatment lasts one year.

alternative_regimens.name: single immediate instillation of intravesical chemotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Give one immediate postoperative instillation for a small papillary recurrence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The recurrence is detected more than one year after previous TURB.

response_assessment.timepoint: At 3 months; if negative, every 6 months for 2 years and then annually for 10 years
response_assessment.interpretation: The intermediate-risk HG/G3 subgroup instead follows the high-risk surveillance approach.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The optimal chemotherapy schedule is unknown. The specified BCG alternative consists of induction and three-weekly instillations at 3, 6 and 12 months.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients in the high-risk group.
decision_rules: Offer full-dose intravesical BCG and discuss immediate RC.
Balance any added recurrence benefit from the second and third maintenance years against costs, adverse effects and access to BCG.
Discuss the case in a multidisciplinary board when possible.

recommended_regimens.name: BCG
recommended_regimens.summary: Give full-dose intravesical induction and maintenance after TURB. Maintenance is required for optimal efficacy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: An EORTC GUCG meta-analysis reported progression in 9.8% of BCG recipients versus 13.8% of controls at a median follow-up of 2.5 years, corresponding to a 27% reduction in the odds of progression. A trial reported fewer recurrences with three years rather than one year of maintenance in high-risk patients, without a difference in progression or OS.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: One to three years: six-weekly induction instillations followed by three-weekly maintenance instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months, as applicable

alternative_regimens.name: immediate radical cystectomy (RC)
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss immediate surgery as an oncologically safe approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider alongside the patient’s high progression risk, potential surgical complications, effects on QoL and possibility of overtreatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: At 3 months; if negative, every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months until 5 years, then annually lifelong
response_assessment.interpretation: Prompt identification of HG/G3 or muscle-invasive recurrence is important.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Regular long-term upper-tract imaging with CT urography is advised. The tabulated imaging schedule specifies annual CT up to 5 years, then CT every 2 years up to 10 years.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients in the very high-risk group.
decision_rules: Discuss immediate RC because progression risk is extremely high.
Offer full-dose intravesical BCG as an option, particularly when RC is declined or the patient is unfit for surgery.
Discuss the case in a multidisciplinary board when possible.

recommended_regimens.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer and discuss immediate RC, weighing oncological benefit against morbidity and QoL effects through shared decision-making.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Among patients undergoing RC before progression to MIBC, five-year DFS exceeds 80%. The guideline reports ten-year progression risks of 53.1 and 58.6% for the very high-risk group according to the 2021 EAU NMIBC scoring model.

alternative_regimens.name: BCG
alternative_regimens.summary: Offer full-dose intravesical induction and maintenance as a bladder-preserving option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Particularly for selected patients who decline RC or are unfit for it; treatment lasts one to three years.

response_assessment.timepoint: At 3 months; if negative, every 3 months for 2 years, every 6 months until 5 years, then annually lifelong
response_assessment.interpretation: This surveillance schedule applies to patients treated conservatively.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For conservatively treated patients, obtain regular long-term upper-tract imaging with CT urography.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with histologically confirmed CIS, including patients with concurrent TaT1 tumours.
decision_rules: Provide treatment beyond endoscopic procedures: intravesical BCG or RC.
Account for the increased recurrence and progression risks when CIS accompanies a TaT1 tumour.

recommended_regimens.name: BCG
recommended_regimens.summary: Intravesical BCG with maintenance increases complete response and the proportion remaining disease-free and reduces progression compared with intravesical chemotherapy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Retrospective CIS cohorts reported complete response of 72−93% with BCG versus 48% with intravesical chemotherapy. A clinical-trial meta-analysis found a 59% reduction in the odds of treatment failure with BCG; an EORTC-GUCG meta-analysis reported a 35% reduction in progression risk with BCG in a subgroup of 403 patients with CIS.

alternative_regimens.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
alternative_regimens.summary: Immediate surgery is another treatment option and yields excellent tumour-specific survival.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Discuss the possibility of overtreating a substantial proportion of patients.

response_assessment.timepoint: Three months after TURB and during subsequent risk-adapted follow-up
response_assessment.interpretation: Response to intravesical treatment is an important prognostic factor for later progression and bladder-cancer death. Approximately 10 to 20% of complete responders eventually progress to muscle-invasive disease, versus 66% of nonresponders.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: CIS may also involve the upper urinary tract or prostatic urethra. A reported cohort found extravesical involvement initially or during follow-up in 63% of 138 patients with CIS.

treatment_pathways.condition: CIS in the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with CIS limited to the epithelial lining of the prostatic urethra for whom bladder preservation is considered.
decision_rules: Distinguish epithelial CIS from prostatic duct involvement and invasion of the prostatic stroma.
When pursuing bladder preservation, offer prostate resection followed by intravesical BCG.

recommended_regimens.name: transurethral resection of the prostate followed by BCG
recommended_regimens.summary: Resect the prostate transurethrally, then administer intravesical BCG; resection can improve contact between BCG and the prostatic urethra.

not_recommended.name: suprapubic trocar-placed catheter
not_recommended.reason: Potential spread of CIS must be considered.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline distinguishes this presentation from invasion into the prostatic stroma.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with prostatic duct involvement by CIS.
decision_rules: Consider radical surgery; evidence from small BCG series is insufficient for a clear treatment recommendation.

alternative_regimens.name: BCG
alternative_regimens.summary: Small series have reported promising findings, but the data do not establish a clear treatment recommendation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Assess individually when considering an alternative to radical surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Prostatic duct involvement must be distinguished from prostatic stromal invasion.

treatment_pathways.condition: tumour invasion into the prostatic stroma
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with prostatic stromal invasion from a bladder tumour, classified as stage T4a.
decision_rules: Treat prostatic stromal invasion differently from CIS confined to the prostatic urethral epithelium or ducts.

recommended_regimens.name: immediate radical cystoprostatectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Immediate radical cystoprostatectomy is mandatory for this presentation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with small recurrent low-grade Ta tumours, particularly those with a history of small Ta LG/G1 tumours.
decision_rules: Office treatment can reduce the burden of repeated TURB.
For selected presumed low-grade tumours, active surveillance or chemoablation may be offered instead of endoscopic ablation.

recommended_regimens.name: office fulguration
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer outpatient fulguration for small recurrent low-grade Ta lesions.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a prospective RCT, outpatient laser photocoagulation with intravesical lidocaine was non-inferior to standard TURB under general anaesthesia for recurrence at four months; the reported pain score was 2.4 and 98% of patients preferred the laser procedure.

alternative_regimens.name: laser vaporisation
alternative_regimens.summary: Outpatient treatment of small papillary recurrences can reduce therapeutic burden.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A small recurrence in a patient with a history of Ta LG/G1 tumours.

alternative_regimens.name: active surveillance
alternative_regimens.summary: Observation is an option for selected presumed low-grade recurrences, although supporting evidence is low.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use an individualised surveillance and intervention plan; changes in tumour size or multifocality have been proposed as triggers for intervention.

alternative_regimens.name: chemoablation
alternative_regimens.summary: Intravesical treatment may avoid TURB in selected patients, but long-term outcomes are lacking.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A selected patient with a presumed low-grade tumour for whom an alternative to endoscopic ablation is appropriate.

response_assessment.method: Assessment of tumour size and multifocality
response_assessment.interpretation: Changes in these features have been proposed as reasons to intervene; the evidence does not establish a uniform surveillance protocol.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation to offer active surveillance and/or chemoablation to selected patients has a Weak strength rating. High-quality trials comparing active surveillance, office fulguration and TURB in recurrent LGTa NMIBC are still needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected patients with low-grade intermediate-risk NMIBC, including some elderly patients and patients with recurrent disease.
decision_rules: Chemoablation may be considered as a way to avoid TURB in carefully selected patients, but remains a promising approach without long-term outcome data.

alternative_regimens.name: MMC
alternative_regimens.summary: In an update of the DaBlaCa-13 RCT, chemoablation without preceding biopsy was compared with standard TURB; twelve-month RFS was 36% with chemoablation versus 43% with TURB, without a statistically significant difference.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The studied schedule was 40 mg/40 mL intravesically three times a week for two weeks.

alternative_regimens.name: UGN-102
alternative_regimens.summary: A randomised phase III trial reported three-month complete response of 65% with UGN-102 versus 64% with TURB. An ongoing phase III single-arm study reported complete response of 79% at three months in 240 patients with recurrent low-grade intermediate-risk NMIBC, maintained in 82% at one year.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The studied regimen was once weekly for six weeks; long-term outcomes are lacking.

response_assessment.interpretation: This was the reported assessment point in studies of UGN-102.
This was the reported outcome point in the DaBlaCa-13 RCT update.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline offers chemoablation to selected patients with presumed low-grade tumours as an alternative to endoscopic ablation, with a Weak strength rating.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with recurrence during or after intravesical chemotherapy.
decision_rules: Consider BCG after recurrence following intravesical chemotherapy; prior chemotherapy does not diminish the effect of BCG instillations.

recommended_regimens.name: BCG
recommended_regimens.summary: Intravesical BCG may benefit patients whose disease recurs during or after a chemotherapy regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients meeting the guideline definition of BCG-unresponsive disease, including BCG-refractory tumours and specified early HG recurrences after adequate BCG exposure.
decision_rules: Apply the BCG-unresponsive definition to identify patients unlikely to benefit from additional BCG.
Offer RC as the standard and preferred treatment.
For patients unable to undergo RC because of comorbidities, offer bladder-preserving approaches, preferably within clinical trials.

recommended_regimens.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer RC because other treatments are considered oncologically inferior in BCG-unresponsive disease.

alternative_regimens.name: intravesical chemotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A bladder-preserving option, preferably assessed in a clinical trial.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is not a candidate for RC because of comorbidities.

alternative_regimens.name: chemotherapy and microwave-induced hyperthermia
alternative_regimens.summary: A device-assisted bladder-preserving option. In a phase III RCT of patients predominantly with high-risk NMIBC after at least one BCG induction course, two-year DFS was 35% with MMC and microwave-induced hyperthermia versus 41% in the investigator-selected control arm.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is not a candidate for RC because of comorbidities; clinical-trial use is preferred.

alternative_regimens.name: electromotive administration of chemotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A device-assisted bladder-preserving option.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is not a candidate for RC because of comorbidities; clinical-trial use is preferred.

alternative_regimens.name: intravesical immunotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: An investigated bladder-preserving approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is not a candidate for RC because of comorbidities; clinical-trial use is preferred.

alternative_regimens.name: systemic immunotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: An investigated bladder-preserving approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is not a candidate for RC because of comorbidities; clinical-trial use is preferred.

alternative_regimens.name: sequential gemcitabine and docetaxel instillations
alternative_regimens.summary: An emerging bladder-preserving approach that still requires prospective evaluation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: RC is not feasible because of age and/or comorbidity, or the patient declines radical surgery.

not_recommended.name: further BCG instillations
not_recommended.reason: Patients meeting BCG-unresponsive criteria are unlikely to respond, and further instillations are associated with increased progression risk.

response_assessment.method: Assessment of durable response and progression
response_assessment.interpretation: An initial response does not predict a durable response; longer-term follow-up is needed.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Adequate BCG requires at least five of six initial induction doses plus at least two out of six doses of a second induction course or two out of three maintenance doses. BCG-unresponsive disease includes all BCG-refractory tumours and T1/Ta HG recurrence within 6 months, or CIS within 12 months, after completion of adequate BCG exposure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with BCG-unresponsive CIS, alone or accompanying papillary disease, who undergo investigation of bladder-preserving immunotherapies.
decision_rules: Treat RC as the preferred standard; the reported immunotherapies represent studied bladder-preserving approaches rather than oncologically equivalent replacements.

alternative_regimens.name: pembrolizumab
alternative_regimens.summary: A prospective phase II study of systemic treatment reported a 40% complete response rate, maintained in 48% of patients for up to twelve months (n=101). The guideline reports FDA approval for this study population.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: BCG-unresponsive CIS alone or with papillary tumours when considering bladder preservation.

alternative_regimens.name: Atezolizumab
alternative_regimens.summary: A phase II trial reported 27% CR at six months among 74 patients with CIS and a median response duration of 17 months.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An investigated systemic option for CIS; the guideline does not present it as an approved or preferred regimen.

alternative_regimens.name: Nadofaragene firadenovec
alternative_regimens.summary: A phase III multicentre study reported complete response in 53.4% of patients, maintained at one year in 45% of initial responders. The guideline reports FDA approval for BCG-unresponsive CIS.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: BCG-unresponsive CIS when considering bladder preservation.

alternative_regimens.name: Nagopendekin alfa-inbakicept (NAI)
alternative_regimens.summary: In the QUILT 3032 trial, patients with CIS (n=82) had CR rates of 55%, 56% and 45% at three, six and twelve months, respectively, with median response duration of 26.6 months.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An investigated approach in BCG-unresponsive HG NMIBC with CIS.

response_assessment.interpretation: These are the reported assessment points for patients with CIS in the QUILT 3032 trial.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Study outcomes for bladder preservation vary with patient and trial characteristics; the guideline considers treatments other than RC oncologically inferior in BCG-unresponsive disease.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with recurrent Ta/T1 HG disease after BCG, including patients with select FGFR alterations who refuse RC or are unfit for it where specified by the study.
treatment_pathways.biomarker_condition: select FGFR alterations for Erdafitinib in the THOR2 trial
decision_rules: Offer RC as the preferred standard; consider studied bladder-preserving treatments according to surgical eligibility and tumour characteristics.

alternative_regimens.name: Erdafitinib
alternative_regimens.summary: In the THOR2 trial of recurrent Ta/T1 HG disease with select FGFR alterations, median RFS was not reached with erdafitinib [95% CI 16.9 months-not estimable], versus 11.6 months (95% CI 6.4-20.1 months) with investigator-selected intravesical chemotherapy; estimated HR was 0.28.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The THOR2 population refused RC or was unfit for it; this is a reported trial result, not a guideline designation of preferred treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Nagopendekin alfa-inbakicept (NAI)
alternative_regimens.summary: In the QUILT 3032 trial, patients with Ta/T1 disease (n=72) had estimated 12-month DFS of 55.4% and median DFS of 19.3 months.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An investigated option for BCG-unresponsive HG NMIBC.

alternative_regimens.name: Atezolizumab
alternative_regimens.summary: In a phase II trial, the 18-months actuarial EFS rate was 49% among 55 patients with papillary-only disease.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An investigated option; this result pertains to papillary-only Ta/T1 disease, not the trial’s CIS cohort.

alternative_regimens.name: EMDA-MMC
alternative_regimens.summary: A prospective Phase II single-arm study of 26 patients with BCG-refractory HG NMIBC reported three-year DFRs of 75, 71.4, 50 and 25% for TaG3, T1G3, Cis and Ta/T1G3 + CIS, respectively.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A studied device-assisted bladder-preserving treatment after BCG failure.

alternative_regimens.name: sequential gemcitabine and docetaxel instillations
alternative_regimens.summary: An emerging approach after BCG failure that awaits further prospective evaluation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: RC is not feasible because of age and/or comorbidity, or the patient declines surgery.

response_assessment.interpretation: Papillary-only recurrence and CIS-containing disease had different outcomes in a review of bladder-preserving studies and should be analysed separately.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The THOR2 result applies to its select-FGFR-alteration population; that molecular criterion does not apply to the other alternatives in this pathway.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with HG recurrence after BCG that does not meet BCG-unresponsive criteria, including BCG-resistant disease or delayed relapse after adequate or inadequate BCG.
decision_rules: Individualise the choice between another BCG course and RC.
Patients with BCG-exposed disease may benefit from further BCG; enrolment in a trial of a new strategy is another option.

recommended_regimens.name: repeat BCG course
recommended_regimens.summary: An option after BCG exposure when recurrence does not meet BCG-unresponsive criteria.

alternative_regimens.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
alternative_regimens.summary: Select according to the individual clinical situation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Balance against the suitability of another BCG course.

alternative_regimens.name: enrolment in clinical trials
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider trials assessing new treatment strategies.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A suitable trial is available.

response_assessment.method: Assessment for persistent or recurrent Ta HG and/or CIS
response_assessment.interpretation: Ta HG and/or CIS following at least five of six induction doses, without meeting the definition of adequate BCG, may fall within BCG-exposed disease.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Delayed relapse after inadequate BCG includes Ta/T1 HG or CIS recurrence between 6 and 24 months in patients disease-free at the three-month evaluation who received no more than induction. Delayed relapse after adequate BCG falls outside the BCG-unresponsive window (> 6 months for Ta/T1 or > 12 months for CIS), up to 24 months.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with TaT1 HG recurrence > 6 months or CIS recurrence > 12 months since their last BCG exposure.
decision_rules: Individualise RC versus another BCG course.
Consider trial enrolment or another bladder-preserving strategy.

alternative_regimens.name: radical cystectomy (RC)
alternative_regimens.summary: An option selected according to the patient’s individual situation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider alongside repeat BCG and other available approaches.

alternative_regimens.name: repeat BCG course
alternative_regimens.summary: A further course can be appropriate for recurrence outside the BCG-unresponsive window; late relapse beyond 24 months is likely to benefit from further BCG.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to the patient’s individual situation.

alternative_regimens.name: enrolment in clinical trials
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider a study of a new treatment strategy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A suitable trial is available.

alternative_regimens.name: other bladder-preserving strategies
alternative_regimens.summary: Other preservation approaches are listed as options.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select according to the individual situation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Non-HG recurrence after BCG is not classified as BCG failure.

treatment_pathways.condition: LG recurrence after BCG for primary intermediate-risk tumour
treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with LG recurrence after BCG initially given for an intermediate-risk tumour.
decision_rules: Tailor treatment to the characteristics of the recurrent tumour; LG recurrence is not a category of BCG failure.

alternative_regimens.name: repeat BCG
alternative_regimens.summary: One option for treating the LG recurrence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualise according to tumour characteristics.

alternative_regimens.name: intravesical chemotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Another option for treating the LG recurrence.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualise according to tumour characteristics.

alternative_regimens.name: enrolment in clinical trials
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider a study assessing a new treatment strategy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A suitable trial is available.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected frail patients who are fully informed and consent to de-intensified care.
decision_rules: Consider a supportive approach without further active intervention as part of shared decision-making.

alternative_regimens.name: supportive approach
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline raises doing nothing as a possible de-intensification strategy for selected frail patients.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The patient is fully informed, consents, and the approach is selected through shared decision-making.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline suggests that PROMS/PREMS might be used for remote monitoring in this context; it does not establish a specific protocol.

special_populations.considerations: The proportion of bladder cancer confined to the mucosa or submucosa at presentation is higher in this group than the approximately 75% reported across all ages.
BCG was less effective in this age group, although it remained more effective than epirubicin in an elderly cohort. Older patients did not appear more likely to stop BCG because of side effects.

The guideline calls for realistic care and shared decisions that account for treatment burden and quality of life. Chemoablation could help selected elderly patients with intermediate-risk NMIBC avoid TURB. For selected frail patients, the panel raises the possibility of foregoing intervention and providing supportive care, potentially with remote monitoring using PROMs/PREMs.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider chemoablation in selected elderly patients with intermediate-risk NMIBC; for selected frail patients, consider a supportive approach rather than intervention.

special_populations.considerations: BCG requires caution: immunosuppression, including HIV infection, is a relative contraindication. Small studies reported similar efficacy and no increase in complications compared with patients who were not immunocompromised. The role of preventive anti-tuberculosis medication remains unclear.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use BCG with caution; no specific dose adjustment is given.

special_populations.considerations: The guideline states that these patients can receive BCG safely.

special_populations.population: Patients with BCG-unresponsive tumours who are unfit for or decline RC
special_populations.considerations: RC is the preferred standard; other treatments are considered oncologically inferior. Comorbidity can preclude surgery, and some patients decline it.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For patients who cannot undergo RC because of comorbidities, offer bladder-preserving strategies, preferably in clinical trials. Sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel is described as an emerging approach when surgery is infeasible because of age or comorbidity, or is declined; it awaits prospective evaluation.

special_populations.population: Men with CIS in the prostatic urethra
special_populations.considerations: CIS limited to the epithelial lining must be distinguished from prostatic stromal invasion, for which immediate radical cystoprostatectomy is mandatory. Evidence for BCG in prostatic duct involvement comes only from small series and is insufficient for a clear treatment recommendation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: If bladder preservation is considered for epithelial-lining CIS, offer transurethral resection of the prostate followed by intravesical BCG. Consider radical surgery for prostatic duct involvement. Do not use a suprapubic trocar-placed catheter because of the potential spread of CIS.

recommendations.statement: Classify the depth of tumour invasion using the 2017 Tumour, Node, Metastasis Classification (TNM) system.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder cancer classification

recommendations.statement: When the lamina propria has been sampled adequately, report the T1 sub-stage using either micrometric (T1e and T1m) or histo-anatomic (T1a and T1b) principles.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder cancer classification

recommendations.statement: Grade tumours with both the WHO 1973 and WHO 2004/2022 classification systems, or with a hybrid system.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder cancer classification

recommendations.statement: Avoid the designation ‘superficial’ bladder cancer.
recommendations.rationale: The designation does not correctly characterise this group of tumours.
recommendations.source_heading: 4.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder cancer classification

recommendations.statement: Obtain a history that concentrates on haematuria and urinary tract symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: For the initial assessment of haematuria, use renal and bladder ultrasound and/or computed tomography-intravenous urography (CT-IVU).
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: After a bladder tumour is identified, obtain CT urography in selected patients, such as those with a trigonal tumour or multiple- or high-risk tumours.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: When MRI is used to stage bladder cancer locally, perform it before TURB.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: Perform cystoscopy when symptoms suggest bladder cancer and during surveillance; neither cytology nor another non-invasive test can take its place.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: Use a flexible cystoscope for women and men when one is available. In men, apply irrigation ‘bag squeeze’ as the instrument passes the proximal urethra to lessen pain.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: At cystoscopy, document tumour location, size, number and appearance, along with mucosal abnormalities, on a bladder diagram.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: Add voided urine cytology to cystoscopy to help identify high-grade tumour.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: For cytology, use at least 25 mL of fresh urine or an adequately fixed specimen; avoid first morning urine because cytolysis is frequent.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: Report urinary cytology with the Paris System 2nd Edn.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer

recommendations.statement: For suspected bladder cancer, undertake TURB and pathological assessment of the specimens as the diagnostic procedure and first treatment step.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Carry out TURB in ordered steps: perform bimanual palpation under anaesthesia before and after the procedure; introduce the resectoscope under direct vision while examining the entire urethra; inspect all bladder urothelium; obtain prostatic urethral and cold-cup bladder biopsies when indicated; resect the tumour; document findings, including the visual assessment of grade and stage, in the operative record; and describe specimens precisely for pathological assessment.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Resect the tumour en-bloc or in separate fractions comprising its exophytic portion, the underlying bladder wall and the margins of the resection site.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Minimise cauterisation during TURB to preserve tissue quality.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Biopsy urothelium that appears abnormal.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: With positive urine cytology despite normal-appearing urothelium, obtain mapping biopsies from the trigone, bladder dome and right, left, anterior and posterior bladder walls, or use fluorescence-guided (PDD) biopsies.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Sample the prostatic urethra when urine cytology is positive but no bladder tumour is evident, or when the prostatic urethra has visible abnormalities.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: Obtain a prostatic urethral biopsy for a bladder neck tumour, suspected bladder CIS and/or T1 disease. If it was omitted initially, obtain it during a second resection when that resection is required.
recommendations.source_heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report

recommendations.statement: When available, use fluorescence cystoscopy or narrow-band imaging during TURB to improve tumour visualisation.

rows: Perform a transurethral resection of the bladder tumour (TURB) followed by pathology investigation of the obtained specimen(s) as a diagnostic procedure and initial treatment step in patients suspected of having bladder cancer.
Perform en-bloc resection or resection in fractions (exophytic part of the tumour, the underlying bladder wall and the edges of the resection area).
Avoid cauterisation as much as possible during TURB to avoid tissue deterioration.

Take multiple biopsies (mapping biopsies from the trigone, bladder dome, right, left, anterior and posterior bladder wall) or perform fluorescence-guided (PDD) biopsies, in case of normal looking urothelium and positive urine cytology.
Take a sample of the prostatic urethra if there is positive urine cytology without evidence of tumour in the bladder, or if abnormalities of the prostatic urethra are visible (see Section 5.11.2).

Take a sample biopsy of the prostatic urethra in cases of bladder neck tumour, suspicion of bladder carcinoma in situ (CIS) and/or T1 disease. If a sample was not taken during the initial procedure, it should be performed at the time of second resection, if the latter is needed (see Section 5.11.2).
Use methods to improve tumour visualisation (fluorescence cystoscopy, narrow-band imaging) during TURB, if available.

Refer the specimens from different biopsies and resection fractions to the pathologist in separately labelled containers. Submit the tumour base separately especially in large and multifocal tumours or when en-bloc resection is not feasible.
The TURB record must describe tumour location, appearance, size and multifocality, all steps of the procedure, extent, macroscopic completeness of resection as well as any complications.

In patients with positive cytology, but negative cystoscopy, exclude an upper tract urothelial carcinoma, CIS in the bladder (by mapping biopsies or PDD-guided biopsies) and tumour in the prostatic urethra (by prostatic urethra biopsy).
If indicated, perform a second TURB within two to six weeks after the initial resection. This second TURB should include resection of the primary tumour site.
Record the pathology results of the second TURB as it reflects the quality of the initial resection.
Inform the pathologist of prior treatments (intravesical therapy, radiotherapy, etc.).
The pathological report should specify tumour location, tumour grade and stage, lymphovascular invasion, subtypes of urothelial carcinoma, presence of CIS and detrusor muscle.

document_sections.heading: 1.1 Aim and scope
document_sections.content: The 2025 European Association of Urology (EAU) guidance addresses the clinical management of Non-muscle-invasive Bladder Cancer (TaT1 and CIS), generally restricting its discussion to urothelial carcinoma (UC) unless stated otherwise. Its practical recommendations emphasize clinical presentation. Separate EAU guidance covers upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC), muscle-invasive and metastatic bladder cancer (MIBC), and primary urethral carcinoma. The recommendations represent the evidence available to the panel, but following them does not guarantee the best outcome for an individual. Clinical expertise, patients’ values and preferences, and individual circumstances remain essential; the guidance is neither a mandate nor a legal standard of care.

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Panel composition
document_sections.content: An international, multidisciplinary panel developed the guidance. It includes urologists, uro-oncologists, a pathologist and a patient representative, selected for their expertise and their relevance to the care of people with suspected bladder cancer.

document_sections.heading: 1.4.1 Publication history
document_sections.content: EAU bladder cancer guidance was first issued in 2000 and is assessed annually against newly published research. The 2025 NMIBC edition makes a limited update to the 2024 edition.

document_sections.heading: 1.4.2 Summary of changes
document_sections.content: A structured appraisal incorporated 36 updated studies across the guidance. Changes address MRI timing before local staging, flexible cystoscopy in men and women, prognostic factors for histological subtypes, definitions and treatment of recurrence during or after BCG, active surveillance, multiplex urinary markers in follow-up, and pragmatic de-intensification.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Data Identification
document_sections.content: The 2025 update used a broad structured search of Medline, EMBASE and the Cochrane Libraries for material dated between the 1st May 2023 and 1st May 2024. Reviewers retrieved and screened 743 unique records and added 36 references. Chapters 3 through 6 assessed levels of evidence using the 2009 Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (CEBM) Levels of Evidence; chapters 7 and 8 used a modified version. Recommendation strength reflects evidence quality and certainty, effect size, the balance of benefit and harm, and patients’ values and preferences. Strong recommendations generally reflect better evidence and/or a favorable benefit–harm and preference balance; Weak recommendations can reflect poorer evidence, uncertain balance, or variable preferences.

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Review
document_sections.content: The 2024 edition underwent peer review before publication.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Future goals
document_sections.content: The panel is conducting two individual patient data analyses: one to validate definitions of BCG failure and BCG-unresponsive disease in non-muscle-invasive bladder UC, and another to examine BCG’s effect on progression in the BCG-treated subgroup of the cohort underlying the 2021 risk stratification. Their findings are intended for a future update.

document_sections.heading: 3.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Bladder cancer (BC) ranks seventh among cancers diagnosed in men worldwide and tenth across both genders. Worldwide age-standardised incidence per 100,000 person/years is 9.5 in men and 2.4 in women; European Union rates are 20 and 4.6, respectively. Worldwide age-standardised mortality per 100,000 person/years is 3.3 in men versus 0.86 in women. Rates vary with exposures, detection and diagnostic practices, access to and delivery of care, and differences in data quality and methods. Some registries show declining incidence and mortality, possibly because causative exposures have diminished. Approximately 75% of patients present with mucosal Ta or CIS, or submucosal T1 disease; the proportion is higher below age < 40 years. TaT1 and CIS remain prevalent because many patients survive long term and have lower cancer-specific mortality than patients with T2-4 disease.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1.1 Tobacco
document_sections.content: Smoking is the leading BC risk factor and accounts for approximately 50% of cases. Renally excreted aromatic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in smoke are implicated. Risk rises with smoking duration and intensity; low-tar cigarettes do not reduce it. Risk from electronic cigarettes remains inadequately assessed, although carcinogens have been found in users’ urine. Passive smoke exposure is also associated with increased risk.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.1.2 Occupational exposure
document_sections.content: Workplace exposure to aromatic amines, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and chlorinated hydrocarbons is the second leading risk factor, accounting for about 10% of cases; relevant industries process paints, dyes, metals and petroleum. Workplace protections have reduced this risk in developed industrial settings, where chemical workers no longer have higher BC incidence than the general population. Greater exposure to diesel exhaust has been proposed as a significant risk factor (odds ratio [OR]: 1.61; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.08–2.40). In a registry study of over one million people followed for 21 years, residents of Israel’s petrochemical Haifa Bay Area had significantly greater incidence of several cancers, including BC, than non-residents (hazard ratio [HR] 1.11; 95% CI: 1.01–1.23).

document_sections.heading: 3.2.2 Genetic
document_sections.content: Family history alone appears to have limited influence, although smoking and alcohol appear to significantly increase BC risk among people with affected relatives. No clinically relevant genetic alteration has yet been linked to BC. Inherited susceptibility to other exposures might explain clustering among first- and second-degree relatives (HR: 1.69; 95% CI: 1.47−1.95). A recent study identified three single nucleotide polymorphisms associated with aggressive NMIBC. Evidence is currently insufficient to support genetic screening for BC.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.3 Dietary habits
document_sections.content: Diet appears to have limited influence on BC risk. Flavonoids have been proposed as protective. A Mediterranean diet has been associated with some risk reduction (HR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.77−0.93), whereas a Western diet and organ meat increased risk in a recent meta-analysis. Higher fruit consumption has been proposed as protective, with a significant finding only among women (HR: 0.92; 95% CI: 0.85–0.99). In the BLEND study, moderate or high consumption of vitamins B1, B2 and energy-metabolism-related vitamins was associated with increased risk in men; high intake of the same vitamins and combinations was protective in women, except for the entire B group vitamin complex. Different food sources—meat for men and fruit or vegetables for women—might explain this discrepancy. Higher tea consumption was linked to lower risk in men through an interaction with smoking, making its proposed protection uncertain. No supplement has been associated with BC prevention, while vitamin E supplementation has been associated with increased recurrence. Preliminary findings in people with previous BC suggest that a cruciferous-vegetable intervention raising isothiocyanates might reduce recurrence and progression. Definitive evidence that diet affects BC development or prevention is lacking.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.4 Environmental exposure
document_sections.content: The effect of drinking habits is uncertain. Chlorinated drinking water and its trihalomethanes may be carcinogenic; arsenic in drinking water has been proposed to increase BC risk and may act jointly with smoking. Chronic nitrate exposure in drinking water does not appear to increase risk. Evidence linking personal hair dye use to BC is uncertain: a higher risk has been suggested for permanent-dye users with a slow NAT2 acetylation phenotype, but a large prospective cohort found no association with cancer risk or cancer-related mortality.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.5 Pelvic radiation
document_sections.content: Pelvic ionising radiation is associated with increased BC risk. A retrospective analysis of localised prostate cancer linked external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) independently to second primary BC. In a single-centre study of 583 patients treated with brachytherapy, those also receiving EBRT (n=255) had greater BC risk (HR 3.29; 95% CI 1.03–10.52) and higher BC-specific mortality with combination treatment.

document_sections.heading: 3.2.6 Other
document_sections.content: The influence of body mass index, blood pressure, plasma glucose, cholesterol and triglycerides remains uncertain. Available data associate higher circulating vitamin D and exercise with lower BC risk. Schistosomiasis can cause BC. Weak associations have been proposed for cyclophosphamide and pioglitazone.

document_sections.heading: 3.3 Summary of evidence for epidemiology and aetiology
document_sections.content: The evidence summary identifies BC as the tenth most frequently diagnosed cancer worldwide (LE 2a), recognizes several diagnostic risk factors (LE 3), and identifies smoking as the foremost risk factor (LE 3).

document_sections.heading: 4.1 Definition of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content: Under Tumour, Node, Metastasis (TNM), a UC confined to mucosa is Ta, while invasion of lamina propria is T1. Intra-epithelial high-grade (HG) mucosal disease is CIS (Tis). These entities are grouped as NMIBC for treatment because TURB, sometimes combined with intravesical instillations, can treat them. Every tumour still requires characterization by stage, grade and other pathological features. The designation ‘superficial BC’ is inaccurate and should no longer be used; the formal recommendation against it is Strong.

document_sections.heading: 4.2 Tumour, Node, Metastasis Classification (TNM)
document_sections.content: The guidance uses the 2017 TNM classification approved by the Union International Contre le Cancer (UICC) (8th Edn.). Table 4.1 sets out primary-tumour, regional-node and distant-metastasis categories. Using the 2017 TNM system to classify invasion depth carries a Strong recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 4.3 T1 subclassification
document_sections.content: Retrospective cohorts support prognostic value for the depth and extent of lamina propria invasion in T1 disease. WHO 2022 recommends T1 sub-staging, although the best method remains unsettled. Methods use either micrometric T1e and T1m or histo-anatomic T1a and T1b principles. Reporting a T1 sub-stage when lamina propria sampling is adequate has a Weak recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 4.4 Lymphovascular invasion
document_sections.content: Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) in TURB specimens is associated with greater risk of pathological upstaging and poorer prognosis. Confirmatory immunohistochemistry is not mandatory.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.1 Types of histological grading systems
document_sections.content: WHO 2004 categorized UC as PUNLMP, non-invasive papillary carcinoma LG or HG; WHO 2016/2022 retained this approach. WHO 1973 instead uses G1, G2 and G3. Patients shift substantially between the systems: some WHO 1973 G2 tumours enter the WHO 2004/2022 HG category despite having a more favorable prognosis than WHO 1973 G3 tumours. A multi-institutional individual patient data analysis found that the proportion labelled PUNLMP under WHO 2004/2016 declined to very low levels over the last decade.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.2 Prognostic value of histological grading
document_sections.content: A systematic review and meta-analysis did not establish superior recurrence or progression prediction with WHO 2004/2016 over WHO 1973. An individual patient data study of 5,145 primary TaT1 NMIBC patients from 16 European centres and one Canadian centre found both systems prognostic for progression, but neither for recurrence, after TURBT with intravesical treatment at physician discretion. WHO 1973 predicted progression better than WHO 2004/2016, while combined 3-tier (LG/G1-G2, HG/G2 & HG/G3) and 4-tier (LG/G1, LG/G2, HG/G2 and HG/G3) systems performed better than either alone by separating G2 tumours into groups with different outcomes. Among 3,311 patients with primary Ta tumours, PUNLMP and Ta LG had similar prognoses.

document_sections.heading: 4.5.3 Clinical application of histological grading systems
document_sections.content: WHO supports WHO 2004/2022 for clinical use, although WHO 1973 remains in use. Reproducibility between observers and prognostic performance matter when choosing a grading system. The guidance addresses tumours classified under either system; using both WHO 1973 and 2004/2022, or a hybrid, has a Weak recommendation. Figure 4.1 depicts how grade assignments shift between systems and shows increasing anaplasia and 5-year progression along LG/G1, LG/G2, HG/G2 and HG/G3. In a series of 5,145 primary Ta-T1 patients, WHO 1973 G1, G2 and G3 accounted for 23.5, 49.3 and 27.2%, respectively; WHO 2004/2022 PUNLMP, LG and HG accounted for 1.5, 49.8 and 48.7%, respectively.

document_sections.heading: 4.6 Carcinoma in situ
document_sections.content: CIS is intra-epithelial, HG, non-invasive UC. Without biopsy, cystoscopy can overlook it or mistake it for inflammation. It is often multifocal and may occur in the bladder, upper urinary tract (UUT), prostatic ducts or urethra. Clinically, primary CIS is isolated without previous or concurrent papillary disease or earlier CIS; secondary CIS appears during follow-up after a prior non-CIS tumour; concurrent CIS accompanies another bladder urothelial tumour.

document_sections.heading: 4.7 Inter- and intra-observer variability in staging and grading
document_sections.content: Pathologists agree on CIS diagnosis in only 70–78% of cases. Distinguishing T1 from Ta and assigning grade also vary between observers under WHO 1973 and WHO 2022. Overall agreement on stage and grade is 50–60%; WHO 2004/2022 is slightly more reproducible than WHO 1973.

document_sections.heading: 4.8 Subtypes of urothelial carcinoma
document_sections.content: Recognized differentiations include pure UC, which represents more than 90% of cases; partial squamous-glandular or trophoblastic differentiation; micropapillary, nested/microcystic, microtubular, large nested, plasmacytoid, lymphoepithelioma-like, giant cell/diffuse/undifferentiated and sarcomatoid differentiation; other rare differentiations; UC with partial NE differentiation, for which the percentage should be stated; and pure small- or large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma. WHO 2022 treats all subtypes as HG. Up to 14.6% of NMIBC may contain a urothelial subtype. The specimen’s subtype percentage should be reported because it is prognostic. WHO 2022 classifies UC subtypes containing more than 5% HG as HG.

document_sections.heading: 4.9 Tumour markers and molecular classification
document_sections.content: Tumour markers and molecular patient classification have shown promise in prognostic investigations, but no pathological organization yet recommends these approaches for routine use.

document_sections.heading: 4.10 Summary of evidence and recommendations for bladder cancer classification
document_sections.content: The evidence summary covers TNM staging; Ta, T1 and CIS (Tis) definitions; WHO grading systems; their reproducibility and prognostic performance; and the superior progression prediction of hybrid grading (LE 2a for each summarized finding). Formal recommendations are to stage invasion with 2017 TNM (Strong), report T1 sub-stage after adequate lamina propria sampling using T1e and T1m or T1a and T1b principles (Weak), use WHO 1973 and 2004/2022 together or a hybrid (Weak), and avoid ‘superficial’ bladder cancer (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.1 Patient history
