document_sections.content: A focused history is mandatory. The formal recommendation is to ask particularly about urinary tract symptoms and haematuria (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.2 Signs and symptoms
document_sections.content: Haematuria is the most frequent NMIBC finding. Visible rather than nonvisible haematuria has been associated with a higher stage at diagnosis. Lower urinary tract symptoms, especially irritative voiding symptoms, may raise suspicion of CIS.

document_sections.heading: 5.3 Physical examination
document_sections.content: A targeted urological examination is mandatory, although it does not itself reveal NMIBC.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.1 Computed tomography urography and intravenous urography
document_sections.content: CT urography detects papillary urinary tract tumours through filling defects and/or hydronephrosis. IVU is an alternative when CT is unavailable, but CT urography supplies more information, particularly about MIBC, UTUC, nodes and adjacent organs. Routine baseline CT urography after identifying a bladder tumour is of uncertain value because important findings are uncommon. UTUC incidence is 1.8%, rising to 7.5% for trigonal tumours; multiple and high-risk tumours carry greater subsequent UTUC risk. For initial haematuria assessment, renal and bladder ultrasound and/or CT-IVU has a Strong recommendation. After tumour detection, CT urography is recommended in selected circumstances, including trigonal, multiple or high-risk tumours (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.4.2 Ultrasound
document_sections.content: Ultrasound can supplement examination and has moderate sensitivity across upper- and lower-tract abnormalities. It can characterize renal masses and detect hydronephrosis or intravesical masses, but cannot exclude every cause of haematuria or reliably rule out UTUC; it cannot replace CT urography.

document_sections.heading: 5.4.3 Multi-parametric magnetic resonance imaging
document_sections.content: mpMRI may add local-staging information. VI-RADS standardizes bladder MRI reporting. A systematic review found that VI-RADS > 4 predicted MIBC with pooled weighted sensitivity 0.78 and specificity 0.94, with high reliability across centres of differing experience. CT urography, IVU, ultrasound and MRI cannot establish CIS on imaging alone. If MRI is used for local staging, it should precede TURB (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.5 Urinary cytology
document_sections.content: Cytology of voided urine or bladder washings detects exfoliated malignant cells with sensitivity 84% for HG/G3 tumours and 16% for LG/G1 tumours; CIS sensitivity ranges from 28–100%. A report using the Paris system found sensitivity 46% for HG disease. Cytology complements cystoscopy for HG/G3 disease but is not intended to detect LG tumours. Positive voided cytology can indicate UC anywhere in the tract, while a negative result cannot exclude it. Interpretation varies by reader and can be impaired by sparse cells, infection, stones or intravesical treatment, although experienced practitioners achieve specificity exceeding 90%. Digital image processing with artificial intelligence in the VisioCyt test raised HG sensitivity up to 92%. The Paris System 2022 (2nd Edn.) uses the full diagnostic categories No adequate diagnosis possible (No diagnosis), Negative for UC (Negative), Atypical urothelial cells (Atypia), Suspicious for HG UC (Suspicious), and High-grade/G3 UC (Malignant). Its terminology emphasizes HG/G3 detection, and retrospective studies have validated it. A prospective study suggested pre-TURB risk stratification: cytology negative for HG had 93% specificity for LG disease; an HG-positive result predicted HG disease with 92% specificity and 91% PPV. One cytospin slide is usually sufficient. Suspicious cytology warrants repeat investigation because the underlying risk of an HG lesion is 24-53%. Adjunctive voided cytology for HG detection and reporting with the Paris System 2nd Edn. each have a Strong recommendation. Obtain at least 25 mL of fresh or adequately fixed urine; first-morning urine is unsuitable because cytolysis is frequent (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.6 Urinary molecular marker tests
document_sections.content: The Paris system has improved HG detection by cytology. Many molecular urine tests exist, but no clinical guideline has accepted one for routine diagnosis or follow-up. Relative to cytology, sensitivity is generally higher at the expense of specificity. Benign conditions and prior BCG can affect results; required test performance depends on whether the use is screening, primary detection or risk-adapted follow-up. Prospective multicentre studies have evaluated several multitarget commercial biomarkers. After negative cystoscopy and upper-tract evaluation, positive cytology or tests including UroVysion™ (FISH), Nuclear Matrix Protein (NMP)22®, FGFR3 or TERT mutations, and microsatellite analysis may identify patients more likely to recur and possibly progress. Practicality, cost-effectiveness and CE-IVD certification matter before clinical adoption.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.1 Screening of the population at risk of bladder cancer
document_sections.content: Screening studies in high-risk populations have used a haematuria dipstick followed, when positive, by urine testing for FGFR3 mutations, microsatellite changes, (NMP)22® and MLPA methylation. Low population incidence and a short lead-time undermine the feasibility and cost-effectiveness of general screening. Routine BC screening is not recommended.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.2 Investigation of patients after haematuria or other symptoms suggestive of bladder cancer (primary detection)
document_sections.content: No available urine test can replace cystoscopy. Cytology and biomarkers may supplement it to detect missed lesions, especially CIS; specificity is particularly important in this setting. Recent comparisons found CellDetect® and UroVysion™ similarly effective for BC detection and both better than cytology. In haematuria patients, Xpert Bladder® showed higher sensitivity and negative-predictive value than cytology or UroVysion™.

document_sections.heading: 5.7.3 Follow-up of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content: The guidance evaluates cytology and molecular urine tests for NMIBC surveillance in its follow-up section.

document_sections.heading: 5.8 Cystoscopy
document_sections.content: Papillary BC diagnosis ultimately requires cystoscopic inspection and histological assessment of biopsied or resected tissue. Cystoscopy and cytology may suggest CIS, which multiple bladder biopsies can confirm. Outpatient flexible cystoscopy with topical intraurethral anaesthetic lubricant is better tolerated than rigid cystoscopy, particularly by men. Two randomised trials confined to men found that irrigation ‘bag squeeze’ significantly reduced pain during flexible cystoscopy. Figure 5.1 maps the bladder sites used for documentation. Cystoscopy for suggestive symptoms or surveillance, without substitution by cytology or another non-invasive test, has a Strong recommendation. Where available, flexible cystoscopes should be used in women and men, with ‘bag squeeze’ when traversing the proximal male urethra (Strong). Record tumour site, size, number, appearance and abnormal mucosa on a bladder diagram (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.9 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the primary assessment of non-muscle invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content: Evidence identifies cystoscopy as necessary for BC diagnosis (LE 1) and cytology as sensitive for HG disease, including CIS (LE 2b). Strong recommendations cover a symptom- and haematuria-focused history; renal and bladder ultrasound and/or CT-IVU in initial haematuria assessment; selected CT urography after tumour detection; MRI before TURB when used for local staging; cystoscopy for symptoms or surveillance without replacement by non-invasive tests; flexible cystoscopy in both sexes when available and ‘bag squeeze’ in men; systematic documentation with a bladder diagram; adjunctive voided cytology for HG detection; at least 25 mL of suitable urine rather than first-morning urine; and Paris System 2nd Edn. reporting.

document_sections.heading: 5.10.1 Strategy of the procedure
document_sections.content: TURB seeks accurate diagnosis and staging as well as complete removal of visible TaT1 lesions. Its systematic steps establish tumour number, size, architecture, site, suspected CIS and primary or recurrent status; clinical stage through examination under anaesthesia; completeness and muscle sampling; distal ureteral involvement; and complications such as perforation. Documenting visible features and predicted grade and stage can identify candidates for post-TURB single chemotherapy instillation or prompt definitive MIBC treatment. The approximately one cm cutting-loop tip can help estimate the largest lesion. Architecture may be sessile, nodular, papillary, mixed papillary/solid or flat. Standardized complication documentation can aid quality comparisons. TURB followed by pathological assessment as the first diagnostic and therapeutic step is recommended (Strong). A systematic operation—bimanual examination before and after, visually controlled resectoscope insertion and urethral inspection, inspection of bladder urothelium, indicated urethral and bladder biopsies, tumour resection, operative recording of findings and visual grade/stage, and precise specimen description—is recommended (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.10.2.1 Surgical strategy of resection (piecemeal/separate resection, en-bloc resection)
document_sections.content: Complete fractioned or en-bloc resection is essential for favorable prognosis (Strong recommendation to use either). Separate sampling of the exophytic tumour, underlying wall and resection margins clarifies vertical and horizontal extent; Thulium-YAG laser may be an alternative to a monopolar or bipolar loop. Selected exophytic lesions can undergo en-bloc removal with monopolar or bipolar current or Thulium-YAG, Holmium-YAG or KTP-Green Light lasers. En-bloc specimens contained detrusor in 96–100% of cases in reported series, but superiority over conventional TURB remains disputed. A review of 1,142 patients found no difference in muscle sampling, and a single-centre RCT found similar rates of 95%; another review involving 4,484 patients favored en-bloc sampling, and a multicentre RCT reported 80.7 vs 71.1 in favor of en-bloc. Preserving architecture improves T1 staging and potential sub-staging and may reduce perforation. Two RCTs and two reviews found no time-to-recurrence difference, whereas an RCT in tumours < 3 cm found one-year recurrence fell from 38.1% with conventional TURB to 28.5% with en-bloc; subgroups with 1-3 cm tumours, solitary tumours, Ta disease or intermediate-risk NMIBC benefited significantly. That trial showed no apparent difference in progression or complications. Choice depends on lesion size, location and surgeon experience; en-bloc retrieval becomes technically less successful above three cm. Optical enhancement may improve recognition of lesions and margins. Cauterisation should be minimized to preserve tissue (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.10.2.2 Evaluation of resection quality
document_sections.content: Absent detrusor in the specimen significantly increases residual disease, early recurrence and under-staging risk. Detrusor sampling is a quality surrogate and is required except for Ta LG/G1 tumours. Checklists and quality programmes improve documentation and muscle sampling and reduce recurrence. In 2,688 patients, meeting benchmarks for detrusor sampling and a single post-TURB Mitomycin-C instillation was associated with less recurrence and progression. Surgical experience improves results; simulator training is emerging but its teaching role remains uncertain. Retrospective studies link operator experience and/or volume to complications, recurrence and survival. In a collaborative study of 503 patients, residents using checklists more often sampled detrusor in 62.9%, compared with 50.6% for experts who used checklists less often. Table 5.1 provides an operative checklist. Record site, appearance, size, multifocality, procedural steps, resection extent and visible completeness, and complications (Strong). Send separately labelled biopsy and resection specimens; send the tumour base separately, particularly for large or multifocal tumours or when en-bloc resection is impracticable (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.10.2.3 Monopolar and bipolar resection
document_sections.content: Bipolar TURB was introduced to reduce complications and improve specimen quality, but comparative findings remain conflicting and are limited by selection, technique variation and uncertain operator experience. A review of 13 RCTs involving 2,379 patients found no efficacy or safety advantage over monopolar TURB. A meta-analysis of RCTs (n=2,099) suggested less haemoglobin decline and shorter admission with bipolar resection; another review of RCTs and observational studies (n=19,927) suggested fewer specimen thermal artifacts.

document_sections.heading: 5.10.2.4 Resection of small papillary bladder tumours at the time of transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP)
document_sections.content: Incidentally detected papillary bladder lesions that are small and not extensively multifocal appear amenable to removal during TURP followed by completion of prostate resection. Simultaneous TURB and TURP does not appear to increase recurrence or progression. Although reports commonly favor subsequent saline irrigation, a single postoperative chemotherapy instillation also appears feasible and safe when neither bladder nor prostatic capsule is perforated.

document_sections.heading: 5.11.1 Bladder biopsies
document_sections.content: CIS may look like a red, velvety inflammatory area or be invisible. Biopsy suspicious urothelium (Strong). With positive cytology and normal-looking mucosa, obtain mapping biopsies from trigone, dome and right, left, anterior and posterior walls, or use PDD-guided biopsies when available (Strong). PDD can direct tissue sampling.

document_sections.heading: 5.11.2 Prostatic urethral biopsies
document_sections.content: In a series of 128 men with T1G3 UC, prostatic urethral CIS occurred in 11.7%. Trigonal or bladder-neck tumours, bladder CIS and multiple lesions increase the risk of prostatic urethral or duct involvement. Biopsy is necessary in selected cases, preferably from the pre-collicular area beside the veru montanum at the 5 and 7 o’clock positions. Sample the prostatic urethra for positive cytology without visible bladder tumour or visible urethral abnormality (Strong). Also sample it for bladder-neck tumour, suspected bladder CIS and/or T1 disease; if omitted initially, obtain it at an indicated second resection (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.12 New methods of tumour visualisation
document_sections.content: White-light (WL) cystoscopy and TURB are standard, but WL alone can miss existing lesions. Enhanced-visualization methods are under development; using fluorescence cystoscopy or narrow-band imaging during TURB when available has a Weak recommendation.

document_sections.heading: 5.12.1 Photodynamic diagnosis (fluorescence cystoscopy or blue light cystoscopy)
document_sections.content: Photodynamic diagnosis (PDD) uses blue light after intravesical 5-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) or hexaminolaevulinic acid (HAL).

document_sections.heading: 5.12.1.1 Impact on bladder cancer detection
document_sections.content: Fluorescence-directed biopsy and resection are more sensitive than conventional methods for malignancy, particularly CIS. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated patient-level sensitivity at 92% with PDD versus 71% with WL and biopsy-level sensitivity at 93% versus 65%. A prospective RCT did not confirm improved detection among patients with positive pre-TURB cytology. PDD specificity was lower than WL (63% vs. 81%), and it cannot rule out prostatic involvement. Inflammation, recent TURB and the first three months after BCG can produce false-positive findings.

document_sections.heading: 5.12.1.2 Impact on bladder cancer recurrence
document_sections.content: A review of 14 RCTs involving 2,906 patients, including 6 trials using 5-ALA and 9 using HAL, reported less short- and long-term recurrence with fluorescence-guided TURB, without differences in progression or mortality; inconsistency and possible performance and publication bias limited the analysis. A review of 12 RCTs (n=2,288) found lower recurrence risk and longer time to recurrence for at least the first 2 years and possibly up to 5 years. A Cochrane review of 16 RCTs (n=4,325) suggested PDD-assisted TURB may delay recurrence and reduce progression risk, but evidence certainty was low; a review of 12 RCTs involving 2,775 patients supported this finding. Conversely, a multicentre UK RCT found neither reduced recurrence nor cost-effectiveness relative to WL cystoscopy at three years.

document_sections.heading: 5.12.2 Narrow-band imaging
document_sections.content: NBI enhances contrast between normal urothelium and hypervascular cancer. Flexible NBI cystoscopy and NBI-guided sampling or resection have improved detection (LE: 3b). Two RCTs did not find an overall recurrence reduction with NBI during TURB, although one found benefit at three and twelve months for low-risk pTa LG tumours < 30 mm without CIS. A review of 17 RCTs and non-RCTs found improved detection with PDD or NBI versus WL; another involving 5,217 patients found improved RFS with either. A network meta-analysis accounting for single postoperative chemotherapy instead found a lower one-year recurrence likelihood only with PDD-guided TURB, with or without instillation, not NBI.

document_sections.heading: 5.12.3 IMAGE1 S™, and other technologies
document_sections.content: IMAGE1 S™ uses computerized color processing and filters to enhance images. Evidence supporting its four spectral modes remains limited, though diagnostic accuracy may improve over WL. Early RCT follow-up did not show a general recurrence advantage, except at 12 and 18 months in subgroups with primary low- and intermediate-risk NMIBC, respectively. Confocal laser micro-endoscopy aims to provide real-time endoscopic histological grading but needs further validation.

document_sections.heading: 5.13.1 Detection of residual disease and tumour upstaging
document_sections.content: Residual cancer after initial TaT1 TURB is substantial and can worsen outcomes; incomplete initial TURB requires a completion resection. Document initial completeness. A second TURB aims to remove residual cancer, restage the original site and collect missing clinical information, including disease extent or prostatic involvement. A review of 8,409 Ta or T1 HG patients found 51% persistence and 8% under-staging in T1; evidence for residual Ta lesions came from relatively few cases, and most residual lesions occupied the original site. A more recent review of 81 studies found pooled T1 residual disease of 31.4% and upstaging of 2.8%, particularly lower in 2010s cohorts; en-bloc and enhanced-visualization initial TURB significantly improved residual-tumour rates at repeat TURB. Another review of 3,556 T1 cases found substantial residual disease and upstaging despite initial detrusor sampling: among 1,565 such tumours, 58% persisted and 11% were under-staged. Prospective studies associated postoperative positive cytology independently with residual disease and Xpert Bladder® independently with later recurrence, respectively, but require confirmation. A second TURB is recommended after incomplete or doubtfully complete initial resection, absent detrusor except in Ta LG/G1 or primary CIS, and T1 tumours (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.13.2 The impact of second resection on treatment outcomes
document_sections.content: A second TURB can improve RFS and post-BCG outcomes and provide prognostic information. In a retrospective cohort of 2,451 BCG-treated T1 G3/HG patients, 935 had second resection; improvements in RFS, PFS and OS were restricted to patients whose initial specimen lacked detrusor. An Ontario retrospective study of 7,666 T1 patients, including 2,162 re-resected patients, found adjusted improvement in OS but not CSS; selection of fitter patients could explain the apparent survival benefit. A single-centre retrospective review suggested survival benefit among 209 HGTa patients undergoing second TURB, but further evidence is needed to identify benefiting HG subgroups. A review of 81 studies associated repeat TURB with better RFS (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.62-0.97) and OS (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.810.93), without differences in PFS or CSS.

document_sections.heading: 5.13.3 Timing of second resection
document_sections.content: A retrospective evaluation associated second resection at 14–42 days with longer RFS and PFS than resection at 43–90 days. For selected patients, the guidance recommends second TURB within two to six weeks of the first, including resection of the original site (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.13.4 Recording of results
document_sections.content: Residual cancer and under-staging identified at repeat TURB reflect the first operation’s quality. Record repeat-resection pathology to support improvement of initial TURB (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 5.14 Pathology report
document_sections.content: Histological examination of TURB and biopsy material is essential for treatment decisions. Accurate evaluation requires cooperation between urologist and pathologist, relevant clinical information, and well-collected, handled and submitted tissue. An experienced genitourinary pathologist may review difficult cases. Table 5.1 supplies a TURB checklist covering preparation, disease characteristics, cystoscopic observations, resection and complications. Inform pathology about previous intravesical treatment, radiotherapy and other prior therapies (Strong). The report should state tumour location, grade, stage, LVI, UC subtypes, CIS and whether detrusor is present (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 5.15 Summary of evidence and recommendations for transurethral resection of the bladder, biopsies and pathology report
document_sections.content: The evidence summary describes TURB plus pathology as essential (LE 1), associates absent detrusor with significantly more residual disease and under-staging outside Ta LG/G1 (LE 2b), identifies diagnostic and possible outcome benefits from second TURB (LE 2), and supports improved detection—particularly CIS—with PDD (LE 1a). Strong recommendations cover diagnostic and initial therapeutic TURB with pathology; systematic operative steps; fractioned or en-bloc resection; minimal cauterisation; biopsy of abnormal urothelium; mapping or PDD biopsy with positive cytology and normal mucosa; prostatic urethral sampling for positive cytology without bladder tumour or visible urethral abnormality; comprehensive operative documentation; evaluation for UTUC, bladder CIS and prostatic urethral tumour when cytology is positive but cystoscopy negative; second TURB for incomplete or uncertain resection, absent detrusor except Ta LG/G1 and primary CIS, or T1; communication of prior treatment; and a complete pathology report. Weak recommendations cover prostatic urethral sampling for bladder-neck tumour, suspected CIS or T1; enhanced visualization when available; separately labelled specimens and tumour-base sampling; second TURB within two to six weeks including the primary site; and recording its pathology.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 TaT1 tumours
document_sections.content: Treatment decisions should account for prognosis. Several models estimate recurrence and/or progression risk in defined TaT1 patient populations.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.1 The 2006 European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) scoring model
document_sections.content: The EORTC Genito-Urinary Cancer Group (GUCG) developed WHO 1973-based scoring and risk tables in 2006 for short- and long-term recurrence and progression, principally using patients treated with intravesical chemotherapy. Inputs are tumour number, diameter, prior recurrence rate, T category, concurrent CIS and WHO 1973 grade. The model estimates individual recurrence and progression probabilities at one and five years.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.2 The model for patients with Ta G1/G2 (WHO 1973) tumours treated with chemotherapy
document_sections.content: A model divides chemotherapy-treated Ta G1/G2 patients into three recurrence-risk groups using recurrence and intravesical-treatment history, WHO 1973 grade, tumour number and adjuvant chemotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.3 Club Urologico Español de Tratamiento Oncologico (CUETO) scoring model for BCG-treated patients
document_sections.content: CUETO’s model estimates recurrence and progression after 12 intravesical BCG doses over five to six months following TURB. It draws on 1,062 patients in four CUETO trials; they received neither immediate postoperative instillation nor second TURB. Its seven factors are gender, age, prior recurrence status, tumour number, T category, associated CIS and WHO 1973 grade. Estimated recurrence risk is lower than in EORTC tables, while progression estimates are lower only for high-risk patients; BCG use might explain the differences. CUETO BCG-treated data and another long-term cohort also confirmed EORTC scoring’s prognostic value.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.1.4 The 2016 EORTC scoring model for patients treated with maintenance BCG
document_sections.content: In 1,812 intermediate- and high-risk patients without CIS who received one to three years of maintenance BCG, prior recurrence frequency and tumour number were the leading recurrence predictors; stage and WHO 1973 grade best predicted progression and disease-specific survival, while age and WHO 1973 grade best predicted OS. Among T1 G3 patients, progression was 11.4% at one year and 19.8% at five years. EORTC developed BCG-treated risk groups and nomograms from these findings.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.2.1 EAU NMIBC 2021 scoring model
document_sections.content: The model used individual data from 3,401 primary patients treated between 1990 and 2018 with TURB with or without intravesical chemotherapy; adjuvant BCG recipients were excluded because BCG may lower progression risk. Independent progression predictors were stage, WHO 1973 grade, WHO 2004/2022 grade, concomitant CIS, tumour number and size, and age. It is the only available model incorporating WHO 2004/2022 into individual progression-risk grouping. The panel recommends the 2021 EAU NMIBC scoring model for defining risk groups. It predicts progression, not recurrence; a model described under Section 6.1.1 may instead estimate recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 6.1.3 Further prognostic factors
document_sections.content: In T1 HG/G3, reported adverse prognostic factors include female sex; prostatic-urethral CIS among men receiving BCG induction; and age, tumour size and concomitant CIS among BCG-treated patients, 62% of whom received induction alone. T1 HG/G3 in a diverticulum warrants particular attention because its wall lacks muscle. Residual T1 at second TURB predicts an unfavorable outcome. Among TURB-treated T1G2 patients, recurrence at 3 months was the strongest progression predictor. More research is needed before molecular markers can be relied upon to improve existing risk tables.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Primary carcinoma in situ
document_sections.content: Without treatment, approximately 54% of patients with CIS progress to muscle-invasive disease. Reliable prognostic factors are lacking, although studies report worse outcomes with concurrent CIS and T1 than with primary CIS, extensive CIS, or prostatic-urethral CIS. Response to intravesical BCG or chemotherapy predicts subsequent progression and BC death. Approximately 10 to 20% of complete responders eventually progress to muscle-invasive disease, compared with 66% of nonresponders.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Histological Subtypes
document_sections.content: UC predominates in BC, but histological subtypes have distinct prognostic implications. Micropapillary, plasmacytoid, sarcomatoid and neuroendocrine subtypes are associated with more recurrence and progression. Evidence remains limited; retrospective studies suggest more rapid progression to MIBC. Other pathological features modify prognosis. Table 6.1 contrasts unfavorable features—greater subtype proportion, CIS, LVI, certain pure aggressive subtypes, multifocality and residual or incompletely resected tumour—with favorable features, including absent CIS and LVI, focal involvement, solitary tumour and complete TURB without residual cancer. For micropapillary disease, focal involvement using a 25% cutoff has been associated with less aggressive behavior.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Patient stratification into risk groups
document_sections.content: The panel recommends risk groups based on probability of muscle-invasive progression to guide treatment. The 2021 EAU NMIBC scoring model derives its groups from primary-patient individual data. Either WHO 1973 or WHO 2004/2016 grading may be used; when both are available, the panel favors WHO 1973 because of better prognostic performance. Five-year progression probability spans less than 1% to more than 40% across groups. Literature rather than the model’s individual data informs placement of patients with UC subtypes, LVI, primary CIS or prostatic-urethral CIS. Table 6.2 specifies Low Risk, Intermediate Risk, High Risk and Very High Risk criteria; additional clinical factors are age > 70, multiple papillary tumours and diameter > 3 cm. WHO 2004/2016 LG includes PUNLMP. The model excludes primary CIS, recurrence, UC subtypes and LVI; literature-based classification places prostatic-urethral CIS, UC subtypes and LVI in the very high-risk group, and places recurrent tumours in intermediate-, high- or very high-risk groups according to other factors. Table 6.3 reports one-, five- and ten-year progression probabilities and 95% CIs for WHO 2004/2016 and WHO 1973 risk groups; these estimates exclude patients with variant histology, LVI, prostatic-urethral CIS, primary CIS or recurrence, and concern patients not immediately given adjuvant BCG after primary TURB. In a single-centre validation of 529 BCG recipients, high- and very high-risk progression was significantly lower than tabulated estimates, potentially because of BCG. A refined 2022 IBCG three-tier intermediate-risk model considers tumour size and focality, recurrence timing and frequency, and failure of earlier intravesical therapy. In a validation study of 677 primary or recurrent intermediate-risk patients given adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy, progression at one year resembled EAU2021 low risk for those with no factors and EAU2021 high risk for those with ≥ 3 factors; longer follow-up and external validation remain necessary.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for stratification of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content:
The evidence summary states that EAU NMIBC 2021 estimates short- and long-term progression in primary NMIBC using WHO 1973 or WHO 2022 (LE 2b); 2006 EORTC estimates recurrence and progression using WHO 1973 (LE 1b); a chemotherapy-treated Ta G1/G2 model separates recurrence into 3 groups (LE 2b); CUETO estimates recurrence and progression after five to six months of BCG (LE 1b); and, after at least one year of maintenance BCG, recurrence history and tumour number predict recurrence, stage and grade predict progression and disease-specific survival, and age and WHO 1973 grade predict OS (LE 1b). Strong recommendations are to assign 4 progression-risk groups using Table 6.2 and the 2021 EAU calculator; use Table 6.3 for progression estimates in primary TaT1 not treated with BCG; use 2006 EORTC to estimate recurrence without BCG; and use 2016 EORTC for one to three years of maintenance BCG or CUETO for five to six months of BCG when estimating recurrence after BCG.

The recommendations are all rated Strong. Classify patients into 4 progression-risk groups using Table 6.2; the 2021 EAU risk group calculator at www.nmibc.net can assist. For progression estimates in primary TaT1 tumours without BCG, consult Table 6.3. For individual recurrence estimates without BCG, use the 2006 EORTC scoring model. After intravesical BCG, use either the 2016 EORTC scoring model, developed for one to three years of maintenance, or the CUETO risk scoring model, developed for five to six months of treatment.

document_sections.heading: 7. DISEASE MANAGEMENT
document_sections.content: Management addresses smoking cessation, outpatient treatment and surveillance, intravesical treatment, cystectomy, treatment according to risk, and recurrence after intravesical therapy.

document_sections.heading: 7.1 Counselling of smoking cessation
document_sections.content: Smoking increases NMIBC recurrence and progression and mortality among patients with BC. In a systematic-review subgroup of 4,405 patients, current smokers had a significantly greater recurrence risk than former smokers. Patients should receive smoking-cessation counselling because of tobacco’s wider health risks.

document_sections.heading: 7.2 Office-based fulguration and laser vaporisation
document_sections.content: For patients previously affected by small Ta LG/G1 tumours, outpatient fulguration or laser vaporisation of small papillary recurrences can lessen treatment burden. In a prospective RCT, outpatient laser photocoagulation with intravesical lidocaine was non-inferior to conventional TURB under general anaesthesia for recurrence at four months. The laser procedure produced a pain score of 2.4 and was preferred by 98% of participants.

document_sections.heading: 7.3 Active Surveillance
document_sections.content: Recurrences of LG(G1) Ta tumours tend to remain low grade and non-invasive; progression in grade or stage is infrequent to rare. Active surveillance (AS) or expectant management offers an alternative to TURB or outpatient fulguration. Soloway et al. proposed observation in 2003 after seeing no progression to MIBC; Miyake et al. later proposed intervening when tumour size or multifocality changed. An EAU Young Academic Urology review judged supporting evidence weak because observational studies differed in eligibility, intervention triggers and surveillance methods. The prospective multicentre Bladder Cancer Italian Active Surveillance (BIAS) project found AS feasible in selected patients and reported that TaLG-related prognostic variables predicted success. In a recent study, patients with three IBCG intermediate-risk factors were three times more likely to undergo later TURB than those without risk factors. High-quality trials comparing AS, outpatient fulguration and TURB in recurrent LGTa NMIBC are still needed.

document_sections.heading: 7.4 Adjuvant intravesical treatment
document_sections.content: TURB can fully eradicate TaT1 tumours, but recurrence is common and progression to MIBC remains possible. Wide variation in recurrence at three months suggests incomplete TURB or procedure-related recurrence in a high percentage of patients. Consequently, adjuvant treatment needs consideration for every patient.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.1 Post-operative irrigation
document_sections.content: Two systematic reviews and one meta-analysis suggest that continuous saline bladder irrigation prevents early recurrence. When intravesical chemotherapy cannot be given, irrigation might be considered instead. The best irrigation volume and duration have not been established.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2 Intravesical chemotherapy
document_sections.content: This section examines immediate and repeat instillations, ways to improve delivery, and device-assisted approaches.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.1 A single, immediate, post-operative intravesical instillation of chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Immediate single instillation (SI) destroys circulating tumour cells after TURB and acts on residual cells at the resection site and small missed tumours. Four meta-analyses involving 1,476 to 3,103 patients consistently found significantly less recurrence after TURB plus SI than after TURB alone. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis of 2,278 eligible patients found that SI reduced five-year recurrence by 14%, from 59% to 45%. Benefit was confined to primary tumours or intermediate-risk recurrences with < 1 recurrence/year and a 2006 EORTC recurrence score < 5. SI alone was ineffective with a score > 5 and/or > 1 recurrence per year. Individual drugs have not been compared in randomised trials. Immediate mitomycin C (MMC), epirubicin, pirarubicin and gemcitabine each reduced intravesical recurrence. In an RCT with approximately 200 patients per arm, gemcitabine outperformed saline with remarkably little toxicity; an earlier study with shorter instillation did not agree. Continuous saline irrigation for 24 hours in both arms of the Böhle et al. study could explain its low control-arm recurrence. Preventing implantation requires treatment within the first few hours after TURB, before tumour cells become firmly attached and covered by extracellular matrix. Every SI study administered treatment within 24 hours. Two apaziquone RCTs found no overall SI effect, although a post-hoc analysis found reduced recurrence when dosing occurred within 90 minutes of TURB. Delivery should be organised as soon as possible, preferably within the first two hours in recovery or in the operating theatre. Severe complications after drug extravasation make safety precautions necessary. Teams are encouraged to identify obstacles and facilitators to implementing this Level 1 evidence.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.2 Additional adjuvant intravesical chemotherapy instillations
document_sections.content: Further treatment depends on prognosis. For low-risk disease, SI lowers recurrence and is considered standard, sufficient care; for other patients, SI alone is incomplete because recurrence and/or progression remain substantial. One study found that chemotherapy after SI improved RFS in intermediate-risk patients. A meta-analysis of 3,703 patients across 11 RCTs found a highly significant 44% reduction in one-year recurrence odds with repeat chemotherapy versus TURB alone, equivalent to a 13–14% absolute difference in the proportion recurring. Other meta-analyses suggest BCG may reduce progression; maintenance BCG appears significantly better than chemotherapy at preventing recurrence but causes significantly more side effects. Several intermediate-risk studies suggest SI may reduce recurrence even when additional instillations follow. In an RCT of 2,243 patients, immediate MMC rather than MMC delayed two weeks after TURB, with repeat instillations in both arms, significantly reduced three-year recurrence by 9%, from 36% to 27%. The effect was significant in intermediate- and high-risk groups receiving additional MMC. A revised risk classification in the investigators’ second analysis again favoured immediate followed by repeat MMC, but inadequate treatment in some participants warrants caution. Another RCT, predominantly involving HR BC, found no benefit from immediate epirubicin before further chemotherapy or BCG. The best frequency and duration of repeat chemotherapy remain disputed, although treatment should not continue beyond one year. A review of 16 comparative studies found that most evidence does not support maintenance chemotherapy over induction alone.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.3 Measures to improve the efficacy of intravesical chemotherapy
document_sections.content: The guideline considers changes to intravesical drug conditions and device-assisted delivery.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.3.1 Adjustment of pH, duration of instillation, and drug concentration
document_sections.content: Two prospective RCTs found less recurrence after optimising MMC administration: one combined a higher MMC-dose, oral sodium bicarbonate and avoidance of drinking; the other added cytosine arabinoside. Their contribution alongside alternative maintenance schedules is unknown. MMC mixtures ≥ 1 mg/mL fail to dissolve fully and might reduce bladder exposure. One trial favoured a one-hour rather than a 30-minute MMC instillation; comparative efficacy data for one- versus two-hour administration are unavailable. An epirubicin RCT found concentration more influential than treatment duration.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.3.2 Device-assisted intravesical chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Several technologies heat instilled MMC. A systematic review and meta-analysis of four RCTs suggests hyperthermic intravesical chemotherapy has toxicity similar to maintenance BCG.

document_sections.heading: Microwave-induced hyperthermia effect (RITE)
document_sections.content: Studies in high-risk tumours have reported promising efficacy for microwave-heated MMC. An RCT comparing one year of BCG with one year of MMC plus microwave-induced hyperthermia in intermediate- and high-risk BC found higher MMC-arm RFS at 24 months.

document_sections.heading: Conductive chemohyperthermia
document_sections.content: An open-label phase II RCT of 259 intermediate-risk patients did not demonstrate better DFS at 24 months with HIVEC chemo-hyperthermia than with standard adjuvant chemotherapy (61% vs. 60%); planned treatment was completed by 59% vs. 89%, respectively. The open-label multicentre phase III HIVEC 1 RCT of 212 intermediate-risk patients found four-month hyperthermic MMC using COMBAT tolerable but not superior to normothermic MMC at 24 months. In a pilot phase II RCT of 50 high-risk NMIBCs, HIVEC™ MMC produced early results comparable with BCG: 24 months RFS was 86.5% with HIVEC™ versus 71.8% with BCG, p = 0.184. Further corroboration is needed.

document_sections.heading: Electromotive drug administration
document_sections.content: A small RCT demonstrated efficacy for MMC delivered by electromotive drug administration (EMDA) sequentially with BCG in high-risk tumours, but confirmation is needed before a definitive conclusion.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.2.4 Summary of evidence - intravesical chemotherapy
document_sections.content: The evidence table states that SI significantly lowers recurrence versus TURB alone for low-risk NMIBC and small Ta LG/G1 recurrences appearing more than one year after prior TURB (LE 1a). SI might affect recurrence despite subsequent chemotherapy, but not in high-risk NMIBC receiving adjuvant BCG (LE 3). Repeat chemotherapy, with or without prior SI, improves intermediate-risk RFS (LE 2a).

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3 Intravesical bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) immunotherapy
document_sections.content: This section examines BCG efficacy, strains, toxicity, treatment schedules and dose.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.1 Efficacy of BCG
document_sections.content: Evidence concerning recurrence and progression is considered separately.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.1.1 Recurrence rate
document_sections.content: Five meta-analyses found post-TURB BCG more effective against NMIBC recurrence than TURB alone or TURB plus chemotherapy. Three RCTs in intermediate- and high-risk tumours likewise favoured BCG over epirubicin and interferon (INF), MMC, or epirubicin alone; the effect persisted over time and was also observed separately in intermediate-risk patients. An individual-data meta-analysis of 2,820 participants in nine RCTs comparing MMC with BCG found 32% lower recurrence risk with BCG when trials included BCG maintenance, but 28% higher risk with BCG when they did not. A Cochrane review also favoured BCG over MMC for recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.1.2 Progression rate
document_sections.content: Two meta-analyses found that BCG delays progression and might lower its risk. An EORTC GUCG meta-analysis covered 4,863 patients in 24 RCTs, 20 of which used some BCG maintenance. At median follow-up of 2.5 years, progression occurred in 9.8% of BCG recipients and 13.8% of controls receiving TURB alone, TURB plus intravesical chemotherapy, or TURB plus another immunotherapy: progression odds were 27% lower with maintenance BCG. The reduction was similar for TaT1 papillary tumours and CIS. A long-follow-up RCT found significantly fewer distant metastases and better overall and disease-specific survival with BCG than epirubicin. By contrast, an individual-patient-data meta-analysis and a Cochrane review could not confirm statistically significant MMC–BCG differences in progression, survival or cause of death. Differences in populations, follow-up, methodology and statistical power may explain the conflicting findings. Most studies nevertheless found reduced progression risk in intermediate- and high-risk tumours given maintenance BCG.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.1.3 Influence of further factors
document_sections.content: Two meta-analyses raised the possibility that prior intravesical chemotherapy biased comparisons toward BCG. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis nevertheless found maintenance BCG more effective than MMC against recurrence regardless of previous chemotherapy. BCG was less effective in patients > 70 years of age, although it remained more effective than epirubicin in an elderly cohort. A cohort analysis associated prior UTUC with increased recurrence after BCG.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.2 BCG strain
document_sections.content: Some small studies without maintenance suggested strain differences. A network meta-analysis identified ten intravesical BCG strains but could not establish that any was superior. A meta-analysis of prospective RCTs, prospective-registry data and a post-hoc analysis of a large phase II trial of BCG and INF-α in BCG-naive and BCG-failure patients likewise suggested no clear efficacy difference. Data quality precludes a definitive conclusion.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.3 BCG toxicity
document_sections.content: Intravesical BCG causes more adverse effects than intravesical chemotherapy, although serious effects occur in < 5% and are effectively treated in almost all cases. A registry cohort found BCG infection after instillation in 1%; a Swedish nationwide database found a cumulative reported TB diagnosis incidence of 1.1 % at five years among 5,033 BCG-exposed patients, highest during the first two years and lower in women than men. Maintenance does not increase adverse-effect risk over induction. Adverse effects prompting discontinuation occur more often during the first treatment year; older patients do not appear more likely to discontinue, and significant toxicity differences between strains have not been demonstrated. Symptoms may arise from BCG or extensive CIS; a significant number improve after treatment ends, although delayed BCG hypersensitivity can rarely arise years later. Systemic absorption can cause major complications, so intravesical contraindications must be observed. Leukocyturia, nonvisible haematuria and asymptomatic bacteriuria are not contraindications and do not require antibiotic prophylaxis. Three RCTs reduced adverse effects using quinolones alongside BCG. In one, two levofloxacin doses at six and twelve hours after first voiding reduced high-grade local pollakisuria and systemic fever, without improving maintenance completion or severe BCG-adverse-event risk. Use BCG cautiously in immunocompromised patients: immunosuppression, including HIV infection, is a relative contraindication, although small studies reported similar efficacy and no more complications than in non-immunocompromised patients. The value of prophylactic anti-tuberculosis medication is unclear. Kidney transplant recipients can receive BCG safely. Manage adverse effects by their type and grade; Table 7.1 sets out local and systemic management, including when to postpone or stop BCG, investigate infection and give antimicrobials, corticosteroids or surgery. Persistent severe BCG-related cystitis can conceal complicated UTI despite a negative culture; the Pharmacovigilance Risk Assessment Committee of the EMA therefore places no restriction on empirical quinolones in this situation.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.4 Optimal BCG schedule
document_sections.content: Induction follows the empirical 6-weekly schedule introduced by Morales et al. Maintenance is required for optimal efficacy. Studied maintenance programmes vary, including a total of ten instillations over 18 to 27 weeks across three years; the guideline’s preferred three-year programme appears in its treatment recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.4.1 Optimal number of induction instillations and frequency of instillations during maintenance
document_sections.content: In the phase III NIMBUS RCT, safety analysis after 345 patients were randomised found that three induction instillations followed by two at three, six and twelve months were inferior for time to first recurrence to six induction instillations followed by three at those time points. A CUETO RCT of 397 patients with high-risk tumours found one maintenance instillation every three months for three years no better than induction alone, suggesting that one rather than three instillations per maintenance cycle may be inadequate.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.4.2 Optimal length of maintenance
document_sections.content: A meta-analysis by Böhle et al. concluded that at least one year of maintenance BCG is needed to outperform MMC for recurrence or progression prevention. In an EORTC RCT of 1,355 patients given full-dose BCG, three years of maintenance with three-weekly instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months reduced recurrence relative to one year in high-risk, but not intermediate-risk, patients. Progression and OS did not differ. In the three-year arm, 36.1% did not finish treatment, principally because treatment was ineffective rather than toxic.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.5 Optimal dose of BCG
document_sections.content: Reduced BCG dosing was proposed to limit toxicity, whereas full dosing has been suggested as more effective in multifocal disease. CUETO found no overall efficacy difference between one-third and full doses; one-third might be the minimum effective dose for intermediate-risk disease. Reducing further to one-sixth impaired efficacy without reducing toxicity. EORTC found no toxicity difference between one-third and full doses, but more recurrence with one-third, particularly when given for only one year. A meta-analysis of nine RCTs found fewer adverse events but higher recurrence and other unfavourable outcomes with less than half the standard dose than with the full dose.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.3.7 Summary of evidence - BCG treatment
document_sections.content: The evidence table reports that post-TURB intravesical BCG lowers intermediate- and high-risk recurrence more than TURB alone or TURB plus intravesical chemotherapy (LE 1a). Optimal BCG requires maintenance: six-weekly induction instillations followed by threeweekly maintenance instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months (LE 1a). Three years rather than one year of maintenance prevents more recurrence in high-risk, but not intermediate-risk, disease (LE 1a).

document_sections.heading: 7.4.4 Combination therapy
document_sections.content: The guideline reviews BCG combined with chemotherapy or interferon and sequential chemotherapy combinations.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.4.1 Intravesical BCG plus chemotherapy versus BCG alone
document_sections.content: One RCT found MMC plus BCG reduced recurrence more than BCG alone but increased toxicity; the schedules used the same BCG regimen, with MMC added the preceding day in the combination arm. An RCT combining BCG with EMDA-delivered MMC found a longer recurrence-free interval and less progression than BCG alone. Two meta-analyses found improved DFS, but no PFS benefit, for combination treatment versus BCG monotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.4.2 Combination treatment using interferon
document_sections.content: A Cochrane meta-analysis of four RCTs found no clear recurrence or progression difference between BCG plus IFN-2α and BCG alone. One study found more recurrence with weekly MMC followed by monthly BCG alternating with IFN-2α than with MMC followed by BCG alone. Another RCT found epirubicin plus INF for up to two years significantly inferior to BCG monotherapy for recurrence prevention.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.4.3 Sequential chemotherapy instillations
document_sections.content: Preclinical findings suggest combinations may improve intravesical chemotherapy efficacy over single agents. Sequential immediate gemcitabine and docetaxel was first reported in 2015 amid BCG shortage and limited mitomycin access; valrubicin followed by docetaxel was also suggested. Subsequent retrospective reports examined gemcitabine followed by docetaxel after induction BCG recurrence, in BCG-unresponsive disease, after recurrence not qualifying as BCG-unresponsive, and in BCG-naïve high-risk patients. For BCG-unresponsive patients unable to undergo standard radical cystectomy because of age or comorbidity, or unwilling to have it, this sequence is an emerging approach requiring prospective evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5 Specific aspects of treatment of carcinoma in situ
document_sections.content: This section distinguishes bladder CIS treatment from management of prostatic urethral or extravesical involvement.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5.1 Treatment strategy
document_sections.content: Concurrent CIS increases recurrence and progression risk in TaT1 disease, making further treatment necessary. Endoscopy alone cannot cure CIS. Histologically confirmed CIS requires either intravesical BCG or RC. Immediate RC yields excellent tumour-specific survival but might overtreat a large proportion of patients.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5.2 Cohort studies on intravesical BCG or chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Retrospective CIS cohorts reported complete response in 48% with intravesical chemotherapy and 72−93% with BCG. Up to 50% of complete responders might subsequently recur, with possible invasion and/or extravesical recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5.3 Prospective randomised trials on intravesical BCG or chemotherapy
document_sections.content: RCTs restricted to CIS are few. A clinical-trial meta-analysis found significantly more responses and 59% lower odds of treatment failure with intravesical BCG than with chemotherapy. In an EORTC-GUCG progression meta-analysis, BCG reduced progression risk by 35% versus intravesical chemotherapy or immunotherapy among 403 patients with CIS. BCG plus MMC did not outperform BCG alone. Overall, compared with chemotherapy, BCG improves complete response and disease-free proportions and reduces progression in CIS.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5.4 Treatment of CIS in the prostatic urethra and upper urinary tract
document_sections.content: CIS carries substantial risk of involvement of the UUT and prostatic urethra. Solsona et al. found initial or subsequent extravesical involvement in 63% of 138 CIS patients; survival was worse with extravesical involvement than with bladder-only CIS. Prostatic CIS can involve the urethral epithelial lining or prostatic ducts. These must be distinguished from prostatic-stromal invasion, which is stage T4a for bladder tumours and requires immediate radical cystoprostatectomy. Intravesical BCG can treat CIS confined to the prostatic urethral lining; transurethral prostate resection can improve BCG contact. Because CIS might spread, a suprapubic trocar-placed catheter should not be used. Small series suggest promising BCG results in ductal involvement, but evidence is insufficient for clear treatment recommendations; radical surgery should be considered.

document_sections.heading: 7.4.5.5 Summary of evidence - treatment of carcinoma in situ
document_sections.content: The evidence table states that endoscopy alone cannot eradicate CIS (LE 4). Compared with intravesical chemotherapy, maintenance intravesical BCG improves complete response and the proportion remaining disease-free and reduces progression (LE 1b).

document_sections.heading: 7.5 Intravesical chemoablation and neoadjuvant treatment
document_sections.content: Two first-line chemotherapy approaches for presumed NMIBC have been reported: intravesical treatment before TURB and tumour chemoresection in place of TURB. An older RCT comparing immediate pre-operative EMDA MMC, post-operative SI MMC and TURB alone generated a hypothesis of improved long-term RFS from pre-TURB treatment. Other groups have not reproduced it, and two small recent neoadjuvant MMC RCTs gave conflicting results. Older marker-lesion studies found complete responses after a single chemoablative instillation in some patients, suggesting TURB could sometimes be avoided. Four MMC instillations in recurrent low-grade tumours and six in recurrent Ta tumours produced complete response in 37% and 57%, respectively. In an update of the DaBlaCa-13 RCT, 40 mg/40 mL intravesical MMC three times a week for two weeks without preceding biopsy yielded twelve-month RFS of 36%, compared with 43% after standard TURB; the difference was not statistically significant. In a randomised phase III trial of 282 low-grade intermediate-risk patients, UGN-102, a mitomycin-containing reverse thermal gel, with or without later TURB, was compared with TURB alone. Three month complete response was similar for UGN-102 once weekly for six weeks and TURB: 65% vs. 64%. In an ongoing single-arm phase III study, the same schedule achieved complete response at three months in 79% of 240 patients with recurrent low-grade intermediate-risk NMIBC; 82% maintained that response at one year. Long-term outcomes are lacking, but chemoablation appears promising for selected patients, particularly some older intermediate-risk patients who might thereby avoid TURB.

document_sections.heading: 7.6 Radical cystectomy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content: Immediate RC merits consideration in selected NMIBC because TURB stages T1 imperfectly: 27–51% of patients have muscle-invasive disease identified at RC. NMIBC can progress to muscle-invasive disease, and patients progressing to that stage have a worse prognosis than those presenting with primary muscle-invasive disease. Discuss possible RC benefit alongside operative risks, morbidity and QoL effects through shared decision-making. Proposing immediate RC is reasonable for very-high-progression-risk NMIBC. Early RC is strongly recommended for BCG-unresponsive tumours and should be considered for relapsing HG tumours after BCG; delay may reduce disease-specific survival. When RC precedes MIBC progression, five-year DFS exceeds 80%.

document_sections.heading: 7.7 Primary treatment by disease type
document_sections.content: After TURB, choose treatment chiefly by progression-risk group; in some intermediate-risk cases, the 2006 EORTC scoring model helps estimate recurrence risk. Low risk: progression risk is negligible, and one postoperative chemotherapy instillation is considered sufficient to lower recurrence. Intermediate risk: ten-year progression risk is 7.4 and 8.5% according to the 2021 EAU NMIBC scoring model. Induction chemotherapy, optionally maintained for at most one year, is reasonable first-line care for most; an alternative is full-dose BCG for one year, comprising induction and three-weekly treatments at three, six and twelve months. Weigh each patient’s recurrence and progression risks against efficacy and adverse effects; a proposed three-tier subdivision uses five risk factors. High risk: ten-year progression risk is 14% according to that model. Full-dose BCG for one to three years is indicated, with induction and three-weekly instillations at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months. Balance the extra benefit of later maintenance against expense, toxicity and BCG shortage. Immediate RC may be discussed: it is oncologically safest but can cause complications, impair QoL and overtreat some patients. Very high risk: the stated ten-year progression risks are 53.1 and 58.6%. Discuss immediate RC; offer full-dose intravesical BCG for one to 3 years if RC is infeasible or declined. CIS: endoscopy alone is insufficient; offer BCG or RC. BCG improves complete response and disease-free outcomes and reduces progression, whereas immediate RC gives excellent tumour-specific survival but may overtreat many.

document_sections.heading: 7.8 Multi-disciplinary tumour board
document_sections.content: Multidisciplinary tumour board (MDT) review of imaging and pathology has been associated with altered treatment plans in up to 44% of BC patients, including a change toward or away from cystectomy in 7% of stage T1 patients, often following pathology review. Discussion is recommended particularly for high- and very high-risk NMIBC. Figure 7.1 presents management by risk category; the available figure content identifies age, history, endoscopic tumour number and size, and the worst pathological stage and grade as inputs.

document_sections.heading: 7.9 Treatment of failure of intravesical therapy
document_sections.content: Management differs according to whether recurrence follows intravesical chemotherapy or BCG and, after BCG, according to the category of recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.1 Recurrence during or after intravesical chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Patients recurring during or after intravesical chemotherapy can benefit from BCG; previous intravesical chemotherapy does not diminish BCG’s effect.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2 Recurrence during or after intravesical BCG therapy
document_sections.content: High-grade recurrence during or after BCG is classified by prior treatment, response and timing to guide further management.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.1 Definitions of BCG failure
document_sections.content: BCG failure broadly denotes HG disease during or after BCG. Tumours may be refractory from the outset or relapse after initial response; some evidence suggests better outcomes after relapse than with refractory disease. BCG-unresponsive defines patients unlikely to benefit from more BCG, for whom further instillations increase progression risk. It includes refractory disease and certain relapses; its definition was developed with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), particularly to enable single-arm effectiveness trials. HG recurrence not meeting unresponsive criteria can still benefit from BCG. BCG-exposed denotes the intervening high-risk category. It includes BCG-resistant Ta HG and/or CIS present or recurring at three months after at least five of six induction doses, which does not constitute adequate BCG; Ta/T1 HG or CIS relapse between 6 and 24 months after a disease-free three-month evaluation and no more than induction treatment; and HG relapse up to 24 months after adequate BCG but beyond > 6 months for Ta/T1 or > 12 months for CIS. The classification table additionally specifies refractory, relapsing and unresponsive timing criteria and BCG intolerance. Adequate BCG means at least five of six initial induction doses plus at least two out of six doses of a second induction course or two out of three maintenance doses. LG recurrence during or after BCG is not BCG failure. In CIS still present at 3 months, an additional BCG course can produce complete response in > 50% of cases.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.2 Treatment of BCG-unresponsive tumours
document_sections.content: RC is the preferred standard because further BCG is unlikely to work. Bladder-preservation treatments are under investigation.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.2.1 Introduction
document_sections.content: Investigated bladder-sparing approaches include intravesical cytotoxic treatment, device-assisted instillation, intravesical or systemic immunotherapy, gene therapy, treatment combinations and new intravesical cytotoxic-delivery systems. A review and meta-analysis of four RCTs and 24 single-arm prospective studies after BCG failure found substantial heterogeneity in design, populations, failure definitions and reporting of previous BCG, limiting comparisons of efficacy. More prior BCG courses, refractory or unresponsive disease, and CIS predicted poorer response. Pooled twelve-month responses were 24% in trials with > 2 previous BCG courses and 36% in trials with > 1 courses. Initial response did not predict durability, underscoring the need for longer follow-up. Another review of 42 prospective bladder-preservation trials found apparently better outcomes for papillary-only recurrence—a median recurrence-free rate of 44% at one year and median progression-free rate of 89% at median follow-up of 19 months—than for CIS-containing tumours, with median complete response of 17% at one year and median progression-free rate of 95% at median follow-up of twelve months. The review highlighted possible biological differences and the need to report these entities separately.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.2.2 Intravesical device assisted and combination chemotherapies
document_sections.content: In a phase III RCT largely involving high-risk NMIBC after at least one BCG induction course, microwave-heated MMC produced two-year overall DFS of 35%, compared with 41% in a control arm receiving investigator-selected BCG, MMC or EMDA MMC. A prespecified analysis found poorer responses for CIS recurrence but higher DFS for non-CIS papillary tumours with heated MMC (53% vs. 24%). A prospective phase II single-arm study of EMDA-MMC in 26 consecutive patients with BCG-refractory HG NMIBC reported three-year DFRs of 75, 71.4, 50 and 25% for TaG3, T1G3, Cis and Ta/T1G3 + CIS, respectively. Sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel remains an emerging post-BCG option.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.2.3 New Immunotherapies
document_sections.content: In a prospective phase II study of BCG-unresponsive CIS, alone or with papillary disease, systemic pembrolizumab produced complete response in 40%, maintained for up to twelve months in 48% of responders (n=101); the FDA approved it for this population. In another phase II trial, systemic Atezolizumab produced 27% CR at six months among 74 patients with CIS, with median response duration of 17 months; among 55 with Ta/T1 papillary-only disease, actuarial EFS at 18 months was 49%. The FDA also approved Nadofaragene firadenovec for BCG-unresponsive CIS after a multicentre phase III study reported 53.4% complete response, maintained at one year in 45% of initial responders. A secondary analysis suggested that post-treatment serum anti–human adenovirus type-5 antibody titres combined with change from baseline could predict efficacy. The QUILT 3032 trial of Nagopendekin alfa-inbakicept (NAI) reported CIS CR at three, six and twelve months of 55%, 56% and 45%, respectively (n=82), with median response duration of 26.6 months. In Ta/T1 disease (n=72), estimated DFS at 12 months was 55.4%, and median DFS was 19.3 months. THOR2 compared oral Erdafitinib with investigator-chosen intravesical chemotherapy in recurrent Ta/T1 HG, BCG-treated patients with select FGFR alterations who refused RC or were unfit for it. Among 73 patients randomised 2:1 and at median RFS follow-up of 13.4 months, median RFS was not reached for erdafitinib [95% CI 16.9 months-not estimable], versus 11.6 months (95% CI 6.4-20.1 months) for chemotherapy; estimated HR was 0.28.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.2.4 Radical cystectomy
document_sections.content: At present, treatment other than RC is considered oncologically inferior for BCG-unresponsive disease.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.2.3 Treatment of BCG-exposed tumours, BCG relapses and LG recurrences after BCG
document_sections.content: Studies suggest repeat BCG is appropriate for non-HG and some HG recurrence, particularly relapse beyond one year after exposure that does not meet unresponsive criteria. BCG-exposed patients and those relapsing late, beyond 24 months, are likely to benefit from further BCG. Individualise treatment of LG recurrence after BCG according to tumour features; this recurrence is not BCG failure. Optimal management remains uncertain when high-risk patients cannot complete BCG because of intolerance.

document_sections.heading: 7.9.3 Summary of evidence - treatment failure of intravesical therapy
document_sections.content: The evidence table states that previous intravesical chemotherapy does not affect subsequent BCG efficacy (LE 1a), and that non-RC treatments must be regarded as oncologically inferior for BCG-unresponsive tumours (LE 3). Figure 7.2 is designated as a strategy for recurrence during or after intravesical BCG, but its decision steps are not stated.

document_sections.heading: 7.10 Recommendations for adjuvant therapy in TaT1 tumours and for therapy of carcinoma in situ
document_sections.content: Strong: counsel smokers to quit; select post-TURB therapy according to the risk groups in Table 6.2, using the 2021 EAU calculator at www.nmibc.net; offer immediate SI to presumed low-risk tumours and small presumed Ta LG/G1 papillary recurrences appearing more than one year after prior TURB; offer postoperative continuous saline or water irrigation when SI cannot be given; offer office fulguration for small recurrent low-grade Ta tumours. Weak: offer selected patients with presumed lowgrade tumours active surveillance and/or chemoablation instead of endoscopic ablation. Strong: for high-risk tumours, give full-dose BCG for one to three years, with induction and three-weekly maintenance at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months; weigh the second and third years against costs, adverse effects and BCG availability, and consider discussing immediate RC. Strong: discuss immediate RC in very-high-risk disease; full-dose BCG for one to three years remains an option in selected patients, especially those declining RC or unfit for it. Weak: if preserving the bladder in CIS of the prostatic urethral epithelial lining, offer transurethral prostate resection followed by intravesical BCG; offer quinolones cautiously for BCG-related adverse effects, mindful of European restrictions related to quinolone and fluoroquinolone toxicity. Strong: apply the BCG-unresponsive definition to identify patients unlikely to benefit from more BCG, and offer them RC. Weak: when comorbidity precludes RC, offer bladder-preserving intravesical chemotherapy, microwave-heated chemotherapy, electromotive chemotherapy or intravesical or systemic immunotherapy, preferably in trials; discuss high- and very-high-risk cases at a multidisciplinary board when possible. Technical recommendations: if SI is used, administer it within 24 hours after TURB (Weak); omit SI for evident or suspected bladder perforation or bleeding requiring irrigation (Strong); further chemotherapy has no established optimal schedule but must not exceed one year (Weak); administer intravesical chemotherapy at optimal pH and limit fluid intake before and during instillation to preserve concentration (Strong); maintain each instillation for at least one and up to two hours (Weak). Do not give intravesical BCG during the first two weeks after TURB, with visible haematuria, after traumatic catheterisation or with symptomatic urinary tract infection; these are absolute contraindications (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 7.11 Recommendations for the treatment of TaT1 tumours and carcinoma in situ according to risk stratification
document_sections.content: All risk-group recommendations are rated Strong. Low risk: offer one immediate intravesical chemotherapy instillation after TURB. Intermediate risk: chemotherapy is a reasonable initial choice for most patients, although its best schedule is unknown; full-dose BCG for one year, including induction and three-weekly instillations at 3, 6 and 12 months, is an alternative. Select between them according to individual recurrence and progression risk, effectiveness and adverse effects. Offer immediate chemotherapy instillation for a small papillary recurrence more than one year after previous TURB. High risk: offer full-dose intravesical instillations for one to three years and discuss immediate RC; the recommendation does not name the intravesical agent in that row. Very high risk: offer RC or full-dose intravesical BCG for one to three years, particularly if RC is declined or unsuitable. Table 7.3 lists options by BCG-failure category: RC is listed first for BCG-unresponsive disease, followed by trials and bladder preservation when RC is refused or unsuitable; late HG TaT1 relapse > 6 months or CIS relapse > 12 months after BCG exposure permits individualised RC or repeat BCG, trial enrolment or other preservation; BCG-exposed disease permits individualised repeat BCG or RC and trial enrolment; LG recurrence after BCG for a primary intermediate-risk tumour permits repeat BCG or intravesical chemotherapy and trial enrolment.

document_sections.heading: 8. FOLLOW-UP OF PATIENTS WITH NMIBC
document_sections.content: NMIBC requires surveillance because recurrence and progression remain possible. Cystoscopy at three months after TURB predicts both outcomes and should always be performed for TaT1 tumours and CIS. Later cystoscopy and imaging frequency and duration should reflect individual risk, assessed with EAU NMIBC risk groups or appropriate prognostic models. Surveillance recommendations rely mainly on retrospective data; RCTs establishing whether cystoscopy can safely be reduced are lacking.

document_sections.heading: 8.1 Intravesical surveillance during follow-up
document_sections.content: Surveillance intensity and investigations are considered separately for low-, intermediate-, high- and very-high-risk disease and for possible extravesical recurrence.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.1 Follow-up of low-risk NMIBC
document_sections.content: Low-risk disease is almost always low-stage and LG/G1. A small Ta LG/G1 papillary recurrence poses no immediate danger, and early detection is not necessary for successful treatment. Recurrence is uncommon after five recurrence-free years; after five years of surveillance, consider stopping cystoscopy or substituting less invasive methods. One study found high negative predictive values for a negative haematuria dipstick in two low-risk follow-up cohorts, 0.89 and 0.94, suggesting a potentially inexpensive surveillance approach.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.2 Follow-up of intermediate-risk NMIBC
document_sections.content: Progression risk lies between low- and high-risk disease, so surveillance intensity can be adjusted. A small RCT in multiple and/or recurrent grade 1 and 2 tumours supports cystoscopy at three months, then, if negative, every six months for two years and yearly up to ten years; the Scottish Access Collaborative Workstream has adopted this approach. Because safety evidence for reduced surveillance is lacking in high-grade intermediate-risk disease, the Panel recommends following that subgroup as high risk.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.3 Follow-up of high- and very high-risk NMIBC
document_sections.content: After conservative treatment of originally high- or very-high-risk tumours, promptly detecting MIBC or HG/G3 recurrence is crucial because diagnostic or therapeutic delay can threaten life. Frequent cystoscopy with voided urine cytology should minimise missed tumours. Recurrence after ten tumour-free years is not unusual, supporting lifelong surveillance after an initially intensive schedule.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.4 Follow-up of extravesical sites urothelium
document_sections.content: Surveillance should account for recurrence in the prostatic urethra of men and in the UUT of either sex. Extravesical risk becomes important in high-risk disease; ten-year UUT tumour rates range from 2.8% in CIS to 25% with multiple recurrent high-risk NMIBC. Voided cytology, cystoscopy and CT urography are key to early detection.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5 Aids for tumour detection during follow-up
document_sections.content: Enhanced cystoscopic visualisation, ultrasound, urine cytology and molecular urine tests are assessed as potential aids to surveillance.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5.1 Enhanced visualisation
document_sections.content: Enhanced visualisation might assist surveillance. Two prospective studies found blue light flexible cystoscopy detected 4 to 5.7% of recurrences that white-light cystoscopy alone would have missed. A prospective NBI study found no surveillance advantage over white light alone.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5.2 Ultrasound
document_sections.content: For initially diagnosed Ta LG/G1–2 BC, bladder US and/or a urinary marker may provide surveillance when cystoscopy is impossible or refused.

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5.3 Urine cytology
document_sections.content: Cytology can accompany flexible cystoscopy to improve HG detection. The Paris system emphasises HG detection and cytology’s limited ability to identify LG disease. Cytology is therefore not recommended for routine low- or intermediate-risk surveillance, except in intermediate-risk HG/G3 tumours. A systematic review using Paris-system categories reported average HG malignancy proportions of 40% for Atypical urothelial cells (Atypia), 81% for suspicious for HG UC (Suspicious), and 91% for high-grade/G3 UC (Malignant).

document_sections.heading: 8.1.5.4 Urinary molecular markers
document_sections.content: Urinary cytology and molecular markers have been investigated as cystoscopy adjuncts for HG detection or as tests intended to reduce cystoscopy frequency. Replacement would require detecting recurrence across all risk groups. Reported sensitivity for LG recurrence has generally been low, although newer studies report 40–65%. Assessment must consider recurrence prevalence: even a test missing every recurrence in a cohort with 15% recurrence would have an NPV of 0.85. A missed recurrence has more serious consequences in high- or very-high-risk disease; in lower-risk disease, marker-guided use might defer or replace cystoscopy, whereas a marker alongside cystoscopy might improve HG detection in high-risk disease. Patients value diagnostic certainty more than avoiding cystoscopic burden. Cost-effectiveness, including QALY, overall expenditure and ICER, needs demonstration before adoption. In the absence of risk-group-specific randomised non-inferiority trials of marker-guided use, high-level implementation evidence is lacking. No marker should routinely replace cystoscopy or reduce its frequency. Some multiplex urine markers detecting multiple genetic alterations nevertheless have fairly high sensitivity, especially for HG recurrence, and very high NPVs, supporting future investigation. Table 8.1 compares their targets and reported surveillance performance; Table 8.2 gives follow-up schedules by risk group.

document_sections.heading: 8.2 Summary of evidence and recommendations for follow-up of patients after transurethral resection of the bladder for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer
document_sections.content: The evidence table identifies three-month cystoscopy after TURB as a recurrence and progression prognostic indicator (LE 1a) and associates multiple and high-risk tumours with increased upper-tract recurrence (LE 3).
