Strong: base TaT1 and CIS follow-up on regular cystoscopy. Weak: for low-risk Ta, perform cystoscopy at three months and, if negative, nine months later, then annually for five years. Weak: for intermediate-risk low-grade Ta, perform cystoscopy at three months and, if negative, every six months for two years, then annually for ten years; follow high-grade intermediate-risk disease as high risk. Weak: after conservative treatment of high- or very-high-risk disease, obtain cystoscopy and urinary cytology at three months and, if negative, repeat both every three months for two years, every six months until five years, then yearly for life. Weak: obtain regular long-term upper-tract CT urography for high- and very-high-risk tumours. Strong: perform endoscopy under anaesthesia with bladder biopsies if office cystoscopy is suspicious or cytology positive. Strong: when follow-up cytology is positive without a visible bladder tumour, obtain mapping or, if available, PDD-guided biopsies and assess extravesical sites with CT urography and prostatic urethral biopsy.

document_sections.heading: 9. PATIENT REPORTED OUTCOME MEASURES AND QUALITY INDICATORS FOR NMIBC
document_sections.content: This section considers the effects of repeated care on patients and indicators intended to assess care quality.

document_sections.heading: 9.1 PROMS and PREMS in NMIBC
document_sections.content: Repeated hospital visits, TURB, re-TURB, surveillance cystoscopy and intravesical instillations make NMIBC survivorship consequential for QoL. PROMs and PREMs have been developed to measure treatment and surveillance experience and improve care, but lack of standardisation and heterogeneity mean none can currently be recommended for clinical practice. Clinicians should remain attentive to disease- and treatment-related QoL effects, including surveillance burden. PROMs are important quality-measurement endpoints, and RCTs should systematically incorporate PROs into patient-centred research.

document_sections.heading: 9.2 Quality Indicators (QI) in Bladder Cancer
document_sections.content: Evidence-based QIs and QPIs serve as proxies for good care and outcomes, help translate research and guidelines into practice, and permit objective quality monitoring and service improvement. Proposed measures should be SMART: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Trainable. Scotland introduced a bladder-cancer QPI programme in 2014 and demonstrated high compliance, reduced national practice variation and clinical value, including development of prognostic models. Implementing a QI programme may foster better bladder-cancer care. Table 9.1 lists general and NMIBC indicators covering appropriate imaging, trial availability, smoking counselling, operative checklists, detrusor-muscle sampling, bladder diagrams, restaging TURB within 2–6 wk, risk-based counselling, appropriate intravesical treatment, multidisciplinary review and surveillance.

document_sections.heading: 10. PRAGMATIC DE-INTENSIFICATION STRATEGY IN NMIBC
document_sections.content: Population ageing and rising healthcare costs require effective, efficient NMIBC care attentive to patient and informal-caregiver QoL. Recent quality improvements have coincided with falling recurrence and progression, but also greater complexity and expense, prompting consideration of less intensive intervention for selected patients. Contemporary progression definitions can help target meaningful outcomes. Especially for older or frail people, care should be realistic and support shared decisions; Scotland’s Realistic Medicine programme is cited as an example. Expert multidisciplinary oversight is considered essential to effective care and prevention of healthcare-related harm, with audit, feedback and benchmarks supporting implementation. For fully informed consenting patients, the Panel identifies possible de-intensification measures: omit detrusor-muscle resection in low-grade Ta NMIBC; use cystoscopic prediction to target effective post-TURB SI-IVC in low-grade Ta disease; select high-risk patients for re-TURB; consider AS, office fulguration and/or chemo-ablation for recurrent LGTa; consider BCG instead of cystectomy in very-high-risk NMIBC; consider bladder preservation for BCG un-responsive disease; reduce cystoscopy or CTU surveillance intensity, or reserve cystoscopy for haematuria; and, in selected frail patients, consider no active intervention with supportive care, potentially monitoring remotely with PROMS/PREMS.
